LungGPT: A unified multimodal system for interpretable diagnosis and clinical decision support of respiratory diseases. Respiratory diseases cause significant morbidity, yet diagnosis remains labor intensive and dependent on physician expertise. Here, we present LungGPT, a unified multimodal system trained on 147 million tokens of domain-specific electronic health records from 125,917 participants. LungGPT comprises two modules: LungGPT-Dx for respiratory disease diagnosis and early warning of critical illness, and LungGPT-Ex for interpretable diagnostic reasoning and treatment recommendations. In large-scale evaluations, LungGPT-Dx achieves a macro-average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.852 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.839-0.865) across 22 respiratory diseases, with disease-specific AUCs exceeding 0.900 for lung cancer and pulmonary tuberculosis. Crucially, the model further improves early warning of critical illness by incorporating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning into textual data and integrating computed tomography (CT) imaging features. LungGPT-Ex generates high-quality, interpretable reasoning that outperforms specialized clinical models and matches advanced general-purpose models such as GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 in correctness, completeness, and truthfulness. By bridging precision diagnostics and rapid decision-making, LungGPT provides a standardized framework to enhance clinical workflows and improve patient outcomes in respiratory healthcare. Graphical abstract                     Highlights    •  LungGPT is fine-tuned on 147 million tokens to enhance respiratory disease management    •  LungGPT-Dx accurately diagnoses more than 20 distinct respiratory diseases    •  Multimodal integration improves early-warning performance for critical illness    •  LungGPT-Ex generates interpretable diagnostic reasoning and clinical decision support      Shao et al. present LungGPT, a multimodal artificial intelligence system that fuses clinical features, lab tests and imaging to enhance respiratory healthcare. LungGPT enables accurate diagnoses, early warning of critical illness, and interpretable diagnostic reasoning and decision support, offering a powerful tool to streamline workflows and promote standardization in clinical practice.     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Received 2025 Feb 23; Revised 2026 Feb 1; Accepted 2026 Jun 23; Collection date 2026 Sep 15.       Introduction  Respiratory diseases, mainly including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), lung cancer, pneumonia, and pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), are characterized by high incidence and mortality rates, imposing a considerable disease burden worldwide.  1   ,   2   ,   3   ,   4   These diseases require rapid diagnosis and symptomatic treatment, and progression to critical illness, particularly severe pneumonia, is associated with mortality approaching 50%.  5   ,   6   However, many respiratory disorders present with similar clinical manifestations, making differential diagnosis inherently difficult. In clinical practice, the diagnostic process demands that physicians employ logical reasoning to discern correlations within medical histories, physical examinations, and auxiliary tests to deduce potential diagnoses.  7   ,   8   Manual review of fragmented clinical records is often labor intensive and time consuming,  9   which could lead to physicians overlooking critical nuances and escalating the risk of misdiagnosis. These challenges highlight the urgent need for intelligent systems that support more accurate and efficient diagnosis.  Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled a series of breakthroughs in biomedical applications.  10   ,   11   ,   12   ,   13   ,   14   The field has evolved substantially from deep learning approaches, which excelled in pattern recognition but often required task-specific architectures and large labeled datasets.  15   This trajectory advanced with the emergence of foundation models, particularly large language models (LLMs), which exhibit broad capabilities in knowledge encoding, text comprehension, and clinical reasoning, thus providing intelligent tools to enhance human productivity.  16   ,   17   ,   18   ,   19   ,   20   ,   21   Several general-purpose LLMs are demonstrating promise in their initial medical applications. A recent randomized controlled trial demonstrated that GPT-4 assistance in managing complex cases raised the management reasoning scores of physicians.  22   Moreover, open-source LLMs such as the DeepSeek model show an enhanced capacity to assist in clinical decision-making for both prevalent and rare diseases.  23   ,   24   ,   25   However, most evaluations have relied on public benchmarks, and their effectiveness in real-world clinical settings remains insufficiently characterized.  26   ,   27    The application of foundation models in healthcare is rapidly expanding and demonstrates remarkable potential across multiple clinical domains.  28   ,   29   ,   30   ,   31   ,   32   The recent text-based generative model Delphi-2M successfully reconstructed longitudinal disease trajectories and predicted the incidence of thousands of diseases, achieving a mean area under the curve (AUC) exceeding 0.70.  33   The foundation model Ark+, trained on a public chest radiography dataset, was pretrained by recycling the knowledge of heterogeneous expert labels.  34   In addition, MUSK, a multimodal foundation model, leveraged vision-language alignment to fully exploit pathological image information. It showed superior predictive performance for lung cancer immunotherapy response with an AUC of 0.768.  35   However, existing models are often applied to isolated clinical tasks and lack the interpretability essential for complex medical decision-making.  36   ,   37   It is necessary to develop integrated decision-support systems that can be embedded into clinical workflows, particularly in specialized fields such as respiratory medicine.  In this study, an intelligent system for lung diseases powered by a Generative Pre-trained Transformer (LungGPT) was constructed by pretraining on 1.8 billion general medical tokens and fine-tuning on 147 million domain-specific tokens from 125,917 inpatients ( Figure 1 ). LungGPT is designed to address four critical clinical tasks: (1) diagnosing multiple respiratory diseases, (2) providing early warning of critical illness by synergizing text records with computed tomography (CT) imaging features, (3) generating interpretable diagnostic reasoning, and (4) recommending evidence-based treatment via structured decision pathways. This end-to-end clinical decision-support system unifies diagnostic intelligence with generative assistance and enhances both the efficiency and interpretability of clinical workflows.    Figure 1   Overview of the LungGPT system  (A) The foundational datasets for the system. It included human dialog data with 5.8 billion tokens that were sourced from large-scale open-source repositories including WanJuan-CC and WuDaoCorpora; a medical corpus with 1.8 billion tokens that was derived from research papers, medical textbooks, and clinical guidelines; and 147 million tokens derived from domain-specific electronic health records (EHRs) from 125,917 participants.  (B) Architecture of the LungGPT system. Based on the above datasets, LungGPT-Dx was optimized for respiratory disease classification, whereas LungGPT-Ex was optimized for evidence-grounded generation of diagnostic reasoning and decision support. RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback.  (C) Network structure of the system. The system included text encoding, a multi-head attention mechanism, root mean square layer normalization (RMSNorm), quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) for efficient parametric fine-tuning, a multilayer perceptron (MLP), and a linear layer for data transformation for medical analysis and decision-making.                     Results   Pre-training corpora and clinical cohort  For model pre-training, this study utilized a substantial corpus of 5.8 billion tokens of human dialog data including the safe and high-quality English webtext dataset WanJuan-CC and the super large-scale Chinese corpora WuDaoCorpora.  38   ,   39   Additionally, a specialized medical corpus of 1.8 billion tokens was assembled, which comprehensively integrated authoritative resources from international databases such as PubMed and MEDLINE, as well as the prominent Chinese academic database China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI).  For model fine-tuning, we further incorporated domain-specific data from 125,917 hospitalized participants totaling 147 million tokens. The electronic health record (EHR) data encompassed multi-source records, including demographics, chief complaints, imaging findings, radiological reports, laboratory test descriptions, and follow-up records. Following International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) standardization, we identified a specific cohort of 29,215 patients whose primary diagnosis was a respiratory disease, encompassing a broad range of ICD-10 codes ( Figure 2 A;  Table S1 ). These were further categorized into 22 major disease types through in-depth discussion and reviewed by senior physicians. Co-occurrence analysis revealed substantial multimorbidity across respiratory disease categories, with notable co-occurrence of pneumonia with COPD, pleural effusion (PE), and bronchiectasis (BRO) ( Figures 2 B and  S1 ). Following cohort partitioning, the training and testing datasets showed comparable gender distributions, with male patients accounting for 63% ( Table S2 ). In addition, the age distribution of patients in both the training and testing datasets was similar and the majority of participants were between 40 and 70 years old ( Figure 2 C).    Figure 2   Characteristics of the respiratory disease cohort  (A) A network graph illustrating the relationships between 22 respiratory diseases and their associated codes. Each node represents a disease, and the size of the node corresponds to the number of patients.  (B) A chord diagram depicting the flow of respiratory comorbidities among participants. The width of each flow line was proportional to the number of participants sharing the corresponding comorbid conditions.  (C) Age distribution of participants by gender in the training and testing datasets.  ASTH, asthma; BRO, bronchiectasis; CB, chronic bronchitis; COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; ILD, interstitial lung disease; LA, lung abscess; LBT, lung benign tumor; LC, lung cancer; LI, lung injury; MD, mediastinal disease; PC, pulmonary cyst; PE, pleural effusion; PEMB, pulmonary embolism; PEMP, pulmonary emphysema; PH, pulmonary hypertension; PNC, pneumoconiosis; PNE, pneumonia; PT, pneumothorax; PTB, pulmonary tuberculosis; RF, rib fracture; SAS, sleep apnea syndrome; URTI, upper respiratory tract infection.                     Diagnostic performance across respiratory diseases  LungGPT-Dx, a pretrained model fine-tuned with EHR data, was used to diagnose respiratory diseases. The system performed well in the evaluation of 22 respiratory diseases with AUC values ranging from 0.754 to 0.967 and a macro-average AUC of 0.852 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.839–0.865) in the testing dataset ( Figure 3 A). The diagnostic performance of the LungGPT-Dx model for most diseases reached AUC values greater than 0.800. Notably, the model demonstrated strong discriminative performance for several major diseases, including pulmonary hypertension (AUC 0.948, 95% CI: 0.921-0.970), lung cancer (AUC: 0.921, 95% CI: 0.912-0.929), PTB (AUC: 0.903, 95% CI: 0.872-0.930), asthma (AUC: 0.902, 95% CI: 0.863-0.939), interstitial lung disease (AUC: 0.883, 95% CI: 0.856-0.910), COPD (AUC: 0.863, 95% CI: 0.847-0.881), and pneumonia (AUC: 0.821, 95% CI: 0.810-0.831) ( Figure 3 B;  Table S3 ). Furthermore, the model demonstrated robust predictive performance across the majority of diseases, achieving high top-1 and top-3 accuracies, alongside a strong F1 score, recall, and precision ( Figure 3 C). Specifically, the macro-averaged metrics reached 0.719, 0.767, and 0.763 for the top-1 accuracy, top-3 accuracy, and precision. Further subgroup analyses revealed performance variations across gender. LungGPT-Dx showed superior diagnostic performance in female patients, with a macro-average AUC of 0.881, compared with 0.836 in male patients ( Figure S2 ).    Figure 3   Diagnostic performance of LungGPT-Dx across respiratory diseases  (A) Confusion matrix of the predicted versus actual categories for 22 respiratory diseases. Each cell represented the ratio of predicted to actual numbers of samples, with the color intensity indicating the level of the ratio.  (B) Bar plot showing the diagnostic area under the curve (AUC) of LungGPT-Dx for each of the 22 respiratory diseases.  (C) Radial bar plot displaying diagnostic metrics of LungGPT-Dx across the 22 diseases: top-1 accuracy (ACC), top-3 ACC, F1 score, recall (REC), and precision (PRE).                   When compared with state-of-the-art baseline LLMs based on a 349-case evaluation subset, LungGPT-Dx demonstrated superior group-wise performance, with an AUC of 0.862, surpassing comparator models including DeepSeek-R1 (0.829), PULSE (0.834), GPT-4o (0.825), HuaTuoGPT (0.715), and Qwen (0.672) ( Figure S3 ;  Table S4 ). It also demonstrated superior top-1 accuracy (0.756), F1 score (0.758), and precision (0.788). These findings underscore LungGPT-Dx’s exceptional diagnostic precision and its significant advantages over existing models, positioning it as a potential AI-based diagnostic tool for respiratory diseases.    Early warning of critical illness  In critical care management, particularly for life-threatening respiratory emergencies, rapid and precise assessment is of utmost importance. To address this, LungGPT implemented a hierarchical diagnostic framework for critical illness ( Figure 4 A). The system initially processed unstructured EHR data for disease detection. Then, it employed prompt engineering with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to convert these textual findings into structured information, which was subsequently fused with CT imaging data through AI models to stratify severe conditions. As illustrated in the CoT schematic for severe pneumonia (SP), the model simulated clinical decision-making by systematically evaluating major and minor criteria derived from both textual and visual modalities ( Figure 4 B).  40   Ultimately, this multimodal paradigm not only enhanced risk stratification but also provided interpretability for its subsequent reasoning and diagnostic decisions.    Figure 4   Workflow and performance evaluation of the LungGPT in diagnosing critical illness  (A) The hierarchical workflow of the LungGPT for identifying critical illness. In Step 1, LungGPT obtained primary diagnostic results and the corresponding explanatory content by analyzing the electronic health record (EHR) text. In Step 2, the system transformed the textual diagnoses into structured database information using prompt engineering with chain-of-thought (CoT) and introduced an artificial intelligence model for computed tomography (CT) images, thereby achieving the stratification of severe and acute conditions such as severe pneumonia (SP) and acute pulmonary embolism (APE). PNE, pneumonia; PEMB, pulmonary embolism.  (B) CoT process for the diagnosis of severe pneumonia. The CoT technique was utilized to transform the EHR text and CT images into structured information, which enabled disease diagnosis based on corresponding clinical criteria.  (C) Performance evaluation metrics for identifying SP, rapidly progressive lung cancer (RPLC), APE, and acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD).                   Quantitative performance evaluations demonstrated that this multimodal integration significantly enhanced diagnostic accuracy ( Figure 4 C). By combining CT imaging data with text-based CoT, the model showed substantial improvements in identifying severe conditions, increasing the AUC for SP from 0.776 to 0.802. It also markedly improved the AUC for rapidly progressive lung cancer (RPLC, volume doubling time <400 days) from 0.595 to 0.899, identifying high-risk patients who warrant expedited clinical assessment to avoid delaying treatment. Furthermore, for acute conditions, this integration increased the AUC for acute pulmonary embolism (APE) from 0.714 to 0.802 and for acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) from 0.816 to 0.869, facilitating timely clinical interventions for high-risk patients. These improvements in identifying critically ill patients may support more timely triage and inform targeted clinical management.    Diagnostic reasoning evaluation  Furthermore, LungGPT-Ex summarized medical texts to generate diagnostic reasoning and treatment planning with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and prompts ( Figure 5 A). Three board-certified clinicians (3–5 years of clinical experience) independently evaluated outputs for 600 diagnostic cases. The clinicians assessed the model outputs in terms of three key metrics including correctness, completeness, and truthfulness on a 3-point Likert scale (1: fair, 2: good, and 3: excellent).    Figure 5   Clinical assessment of the ability of LungGPT to generate text  (A) Study design for clinician evaluation of diagnostic reasoning and decision-generation outputs produced by LungGPT-Ex and five comparator models using correctness, completeness, and truthfulness.  (B) Distributions of reader scores for diagnostic reasoning. The heatmaps denoted reader preferences as measured by a 3-point Likert scale. The box indicates the interquartile range (IQR), whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR (Tukey’s method), dots represent outliers, and + denotes the mean. Statistical significance was determined using Friedman test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. ∗∗∗ p  < 0.001. ns, not significant.  (C) Distribution of reader scores for decision generation. The heatmaps denoted reader preference as measured by a 3-point Likert scale. The box indicates the IQR, whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR (Tukey’s method), dots represent outliers, and + denotes the mean. Statistical significance was determined using Friedman test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. ∗∗ p  < 0.01, ∗∗∗ p  < 0.001. ns, not significant.                   In terms of diagnostic reasoning, LungGPT-Ex outperformed most LLMs ( Figures 5 B and  S4 ;  Table S5 ). For correctness, LungGPT-Ex achieved an average score of 2.84, reflecting its ability to minimize false or misleading information. This performance significantly exceeded that of PULSE (1.34), HuaTuoGPT (1.38), Qwen (2.31), and DeepSeek-R1 (2.33), while closely matching that of GPT-4o (2.89). Regarding completeness, LungGPT-Ex scored 2.71, highlighting its capacity to provide detailed and comprehensive diagnostic explanations. This score surpassed PULSE (1.25), HuaTuoGPT (1.33), Qwen (1.84), and DeepSeek-R1 (2.27). Its truthfulness score (2.90) was comparable to GPT-4o (2.92) and DeepSeek-R1 (2.87) and significantly outperformed PULSE (1.43), HuaTuoGPT (1.54), and Qwen (2.59).    Decision generation evaluation  In the task of treatment planning, LungGPT-Ex continued to demonstrate exceptional performance ( Figures 5 C and  S5 ;  Table S6 ). It achieved a correctness score of 2.63, outperforming PULSE (1.18), HuaTuoGPT (1.27), Qwen (2.44), and DeepSeek-R1 (2.45), and nearly matching GPT-4o (2.72). With respect to completeness, LungGPT-Ex scored 2.65, on par with GPT-4o (2.64) and substantially higher than DeepSeek-R1 (2.32), Qwen (2.27), and HuaTuoGPT (1.30). Its truthfulness score was particularly notable, achieving 2.92 and comparable to GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen, significantly outperforming HuaTuoGPT (1.57) and PULSE (1.35).  Beyond diagnostic explanation, LungGPT-Ex generated patient-specific management suggestions spanning scheduled surveillance and follow-up, pharmacologic therapy, surgical or interventional evaluation when indicated, multidisciplinary team consultation, comprehensive treatment planning, and so on. By organizing diagnostic evidence and potential management options into a structured format, LungGPT-Ex could assist clinicians in interpreting model outputs, thereby improving the efficiency of clinical decision-making.    Clinical application of LungGPT  In practice, LungGPT used unstructured EHR data as input and then produced concise summaries including diagnoses, evidence-based diagnostic reasoning, and tailored decision recommendations ( Figure 6 ). As illustrated in a representative case of a 57-year-old male presenting with recurrent cough, sputum production, dyspnea, and hemoptysis, the model accurately identified severe pneumonia—supported by clinical manifestations such as acute symptom exacerbation, auscultatory findings of wet rales, and chest CT revealing scattered patches, nodules, and consolidations in both lungs. Additionally, LungGPT recognized acute exacerbation of COPD and chronic pulmonary heart disease, integrating longitudinal history and multimodality data into a coherent diagnostic narrative. The system further provided clear therapeutic guidance for severe cases, including prioritized antibiotic treatment, cardiopulmonary function support, and individualized monitoring plans. The clinical application of LungGPT was facilitated by a streamlined interface with several steps ( Figure S6 ). Specifically, it provided tailored recommendations for key disease categories including infectious, neoplastic, airway, and interstitial lung diseases. This example illustrates how LungGPT automatically generates structured diagnostic reasoning and clinical decision-support recommendations from complex patient records.    Figure 6   Application of LungGPT for tailored diagnosis and decision recommendations in respiratory diseases  After inputting the prompt command, the system could analyze admission records to diagnose disease. It also generated text summarized to provide clinicians with diagnostic reasoning and decision recommendations. This example highlighted the identification of severe pneumonia, supported by clinical findings such as recurrent cough and imaging results, and delivered clear therapeutic guidance, notably outlining specific interventions like oxygen therapy and anti-infective regimens for critical cases. All generated outputs were reviewed under clinician supervision, and final diagnostic and treatment decisions remained the responsibility of the treating physician.                      Discussion  In this study, a domain-specific multimodal system named LungGPT was developed for respiratory disease diagnosis and clinical decision support. This system was adept at processing information from multiple sources, including chief complaints, imaging findings, and laboratory tests to classify 22 respiratory diseases. Moreover, LungGPT excelled in the timely identification of critical conditions and provided intervention options. Meanwhile, LungGPT was capable of generating diagnostic reasoning and treatment planning based on specific prompts. Its performance was superior to that of most existing models, positioning it as a powerful auxiliary tool in clinical practice.  The rapid advancement of AI has fundamentally transformed the execution of healthcare tasks.  41   ,   42   ,   43   ,   44   A paradigmatic development in modern AI is the emergence of foundation models.  45   Leveraging large-scale datasets for pretraining and fine-tuning, general-purpose AI systems capably serve a broad spectrum of downstream tasks. LungGPT achieved superior diagnostic performance with a notable enhancement after pretraining and fine-tuning. This advantage was largely attributable to the large-scale, high-quality clinical corpus derived from 125,917 inpatient EHRs. This underscores the significant impact of domain-specific fine-tuning on amplifying the capabilities of LLMs.  46   ,   47   However, the diagnostic performance remains suboptimal for some diseases. On the one hand, overlapping features and hierarchical disease coding relationships often complicate diagnosis given the complex comorbid relationships. To address this, top-3 accuracy was additionally reported to account for clinically plausible alternative diagnoses in the ranked model outputs. On the other hand, the diagnostic accuracy for certain diseases was hindered by limited data volume, suggesting that zero-shot or few-shot learning may offer promising solutions for further improvement.  48    Another paradigm in modern AI focuses on generative models, which integrate high-dimensional data to create content spanning text, images, and molecular designs.  45   However, general-purpose LLMs often lack the rigorous precision required for medical applications. Leveraging real-world cases as prompts, LungGPT generated diagnostic reasoning and decision-making schemes whose format and phrasing closely mirror those of authentic inpatient records. The model was comparable to GPT-4o in terms of correctness, completeness, and truthfulness, providing powerful technical support to assist physicians in improving their productivity. Meanwhile, through RAG that draws on authoritative sources including guidelines, expert consensus, and professional textbooks, LungGPT-Ex generated clinical summaries that remain fully aligned with contemporary practice. This ability to update and standardize prompts in a timely manner endowed this model with higher accuracy in the text generation for respiratory diseases.  49   Future developments could incorporate real-time dialog functionality, enabling more natural and efficient interactions between physicians and the model.  50   ,   51    LLMs leverage encoded medical knowledge to aid clinicians toward precision diagnostic efficiency. Google introduced Med-PaLM, which integrated clinical knowledge with instruction-tuned learning and achieved expert-level performance on the MultiMedQA benchmark.  52   Its successor, Med-PaLM 2, further incorporated retrieval and verification strategies, attaining an accuracy of 86.5% on the MedQA dataset, which represented a 19% improvement over the Med-PaLM.  53   In respiratory medicine, foundation models cover a wide range of aspects such as disease screening, diagnosis, and treatment. For example, GPT-4o has been used to evaluate malignancy progression of pulmonary nodules to support lung cancer screening by dynamically monitoring the size and morphology.  54   While models like text-based Delphi-2M and imaging-based Ark+ can predict respiratory diseases, they lack the capability for treatment recommendation.  33   ,   34   In this study, LungGPT unified diagnostic inference and decision support, positioning itself for seamless integration into routine practice.  Guided by the clinical demands of respiratory medicine, LungGPT has preliminarily explored the integration of data from various sources and has achieved promising results in the decision support of various diseases. Currently, multimodal generative models have advanced rapidly.  55   ,   56   ,   57   The integration of multimodal data enables clinicians to gain a comprehensive understanding of diseases to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis, alleviating the limitations imposed by single-modality data.  58   ,   59   ,   60   For instance, BiomedGPT, as a vision-language generalist model, utilizes joint learning of imaging and textual features to achieve cross-modal alignment, which enables it to perform a wide range of biomedical tasks.  61   Nevertheless, real-world deployment confronts formidable challenges. Datasets must be watermarked for full traceability,  62   while hallucinations, biases, and equity concerns that are inherent to LLMs continue to impede adoption.  63   Consequently, clinicians, researchers, health-policy experts, and patient representatives must be integrated from the earliest design and development stages to safeguard fairness and ethical alignment.  64    In summary, LungGPT, as a domain-specific LLM trained on large-scale data, excelled in predicting 22 respiratory diseases and risk stratification for critical illness. It furthermore generated interpretable and traceable diagnostic reasoning and decision recommendations. The multimodal system provides an end-to-end framework spanning diagnosis, early warning of critical illness, and decision support. This system was expected to substantially enhance the quality of healthcare services.   Limitations of the study  The clinical translation of LungGPT confronts several challenges. First, the generalizability and robustness of LungGPT require further external validation across diverse demographic and regional settings. Second, the integration of multimodal and dynamic clinical data is needed to evolve LungGPT into a generalist medical AI agent, thereby operationalizing cross-scale precision medicine and enabling comprehensive exploitation of molecular-to-patient information within an AI framework to deliver truly individualized therapeutic decisions.  65   In addition, progression from an experimental architecture to a regulated decision-support tool demands rigorous regulatory scrutiny. To address these issues, prospective and multi-center studies are necessary to iteratively refine the model.    Experimental model and study participant details  The data used in this study consist of both general medical corpora and domain-specific electronic health record (EHR) data. Specifically, the general medical corpus was employed during pretraining to enable the large language model (LLM) to acquire representations relevant to clinical reasoning. Moreover, we ensured that this pretraining did not compromise the model’s instruction-following and interactive capabilities. To achieve this goal, we incorporated both an online human dialogue corpus and a general medical corpus sourced from research papers, textbooks, and clinical guidelines. Domain-specific EHR data from 125,917 participants were derived from West China Hospital of Sichuan University for the period from 2009 to 2021 and were utilized in the fine-tuning phase. These records included comprehensive information about patient conditions, such as demographic details, chief complaints, imaging findings, radiological reports, laboratory test descriptions, pathological reports, pulmonary function tests, and follow-up records. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee in the West China Hospital of Sichuan University, Chengdu, China (No. 2024.1762). Informed consent was waived because of the retrospective nature of the study.    Method details   Multimodal data processing   Data curation  To enhance the capabilities of models in both general communication and specialized domains, the pre-training data incorporated 5.8 billion tokens of open-source human dialogue from WanJuan-CC (English) and WuDaoCorpora (Chinese). Furthermore, to ground the model in robust medical knowledge, a dedicated corpus of 1.8 billion tokens was constructed from peer-reviewed research and clinical guidelines indexed in PubMed, MEDLINE, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). This general medical corpus comprised the latest clinical studies, specialized textbooks, and practice guidelines related to respiratory disease management.  Domain-specific EHR data were derived from 125,917 hospitalized patients with at least one respiratory disease diagnosis. Eligible patients were those with a confirmed respiratory disease and complete inpatient EHRs. Patients with unclear diagnoses or suspected misdiagnosis, as well as those who could not be clearly matched to a specific respiratory disease, were excluded. Cases deemed unsuitable for inclusion by the researchers were also excluded. A total of 29,215 patients with a primary diagnosis of respiratory disease were included in this study, and the dataset was partitioned into a training set and a testing set at an 8:2 ratio.    ICD-10 label encoding  To ensure data consistency and comparability, we standardized all patients’ diagnostic information by ICD-10 coding, which was manually annotated ( Table S1 ). Initially, we implemented a fuzzy matching algorithm that compared the disease names written by physicians with the ICD-10 code list to find the most similar matches. This step aimed to reduce the annotation workload. Despite the assistance from fuzzy matching, all the coding was manually verified and annotated by our team of experienced clinical coders. This manual process ensured that each diagnosis was accurately matched to the correct ICD-10 code. By relying on manual annotation, supported by fuzzy matching for efficiency, we maintained a high level of accuracy and consistency in the ICD-10 coding process for our dataset.    Chest CT image acquisition  Chest computed tomography (CT) images were retrieved in DICOM format from the Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS). Eligibility criteria included volumetric CT acquisition within 48 hours before or after the index admission, axial slice thickness ≤ 2.5 mm, and complete lung coverage from the lung apices to the costophrenic angles. Patients who met these CT criteria and had complete EHR data were included in the multimodal cohort for critical illness prediction. Severe pneumonia, rapidly progressive lung cancer, AECOPD, and acute pulmonary embolism were selected as the critical illness subtypes for investigation. The role of multimodal information fusion in enabling precise differential diagnosis was assessed across these conditions.     LungGPT architecture and workflow   Task-specific large language models  We developed two distinct LLMs for the tasks of disease diagnosis and decision explanation, named LungGPT-Dx (7B) and LungGPT-Ex (110B), respectively. Both models were based on the Qwen architecture  68   and trained using quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA).  70   The LungGPT-Dx was fine-tuned for ICD-10 annotated disease diagnosis, which significantly enhanced its performance in classification tasks. However, fully fine-tuning an LLM often compromises its conversational and logical reasoning abilities.  71   Therefore, LungGPT-Ex underwent supervised fine-tuning (SFT) separately and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)  72   based on Qwen-110B, enabling it to have a nuanced understanding of diagnostic criteria while maintaining robust conversational capabilities.    Retrieval-augmented generation  The general medical corpus underwent data preprocessing to construct a textual knowledge base, which was then embedded into vectors to form a vectorized knowledge database. The knowledge database was designed for continuous real-time updates. In situations where updating the base model with pretraining was not feasible, the real-time augmentation of medical knowledge through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) effectively mitigated the model’s limitations in handling medical knowledge. In implementation, retrieved clinically relevant passages from the knowledge base. This could provide reference information for LungGPT-Ex in terms of diagnostic criteria and maintain reliable answers.    Integrated pipeline  The workflow of our proposed framework included LungGPT-Dx, LungGPT-Ex, and the structured database. In practical applications, the patient’s EHR was first input into LungGPT-Dx, which generated a textual diagnosis of potential respiratory diseases. Next, the patient’s EHR was concatenated with the diagnostic output from LungGPT-Dx to create a query, which was then processed via LangChain  73   to retrieve relevant knowledge from a structured database. This integration of EHR data and diagnostic results formed a knowledge-enhanced input. This enhanced input was subsequently fed into LungGPT-Ex, which was responsible for providing a comprehensive explanation of the diagnosis. LungGPT-Ex then delivered a detailed diagnostic explanation and generated treatment planning.  To achieve precise identification of critical respiratory conditions, we developed a hierarchical framework that integrated textual clinical data with radiological features. First, a chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting strategy  74   was employed to identify key physiological indicators and symptomatic abnormalities within the EHR, mapping these findings to predefined clinical semantic categories. Simultaneously, a deep learning model was utilized to extract high-dimensional features from chest CT images.  75   Through this integrated reasoning process, the system generated evidence-based syntheses aligned with established clinical guidelines, enabling the high-fidelity identification of critically ill patients.     Model benchmarking and evaluation   Comparator models  To ensure fair benchmarking between LungGPT and the baseline LLM models, we implemented strict evaluation protocols. All the comparator models were used in their original public releases without domain adaptation in our study. Specifically, PULSE was implemented using the Bloomz architecture; the publicly available LLaMA-based 7B medical version of HuaTuoGPT was utilized, the Qwen-7B general-purpose implementation of Qwen was employed, GPT-4o was accessed via an official API without customization, and the publicly available DeepSeek-R1 was used for DeepSeek. The complete model configurations were detailed in  Table S7 .    Respiratory disease diagnosis  For the performance evaluation of LungGPT-Dx, we employed several key metrics including area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC), the top-1/3 accuracy (ACC), precision (PRE), recall (REC), and the F1 score (F1). These metrics were critical for assessing the effectiveness of our classification approach. The AUC quantified the model’s ability to discriminate between positive and negative cases across all classification thresholds, with higher values indicating better overall diagnostic performance. Top-1/3 ACC measured the frequency with which the correct diagnosis appears within the top 1 or 3 predictions made by the model. They provide a clear picture of the model’s ranking ability, with top-1 accuracy being the strictest measure and top-3 accuracy offering a broader view of the model’s capabilities. PRE was the ratio of the number of correctly predicted positive observations to the total number of predicted positive observations. It is a measure of the model’s accuracy in identifying relevant instances among the retrieved instances. REC or sensitivity, was the ratio of the number of correctly predicted positive observations to the total number of observations in the actual class. It assesses the model’s ability to identify all relevant instances. The F1 score was the harmonic mean of precision and recall, and it provided a single metric that balanced concerns regarding both false positives and false negatives. It is particularly useful when dealing with imbalanced datasets.    Diagnostic reasoning and decision support  Considering the evaluation of the diagnostic criteria provided by the LungGPT-Ex, we adopted the Likert Scale Scoring system. The Likert scale was a widely recognized psychometric tool used to gauge subjective assessments, where respondents specify their level of agreement or disagreement with a statement.  Correctness, completeness, and truthfulness were the key evaluation indicators for the responses of LLMs. Correctness was used to evaluate whether the diagnostic criteria can support the diagnostic result accurately to ensure alignment with established medical knowledge. Completeness measured whether the diagnostic criteria cover all necessary aspects needed to reach a proper diagnosis and was used to assess the thoroughness of the LLM’s output. Truthfulness was used to assess whether the diagnostic criteria are based on real and verifiable information to ensure the reliability and trustworthiness of the information provided by the LLM. Each criterion was assessed on a 3-point scale, where 3 represents the best score and 1 represents the worst score.  By combining these quantitative and qualitative evaluation methods, we aimed to thoroughly assess the performance and reliability of this proposed method for respiratory disease diagnosis and to ensure that it meets the high standards required for clinical application.     Implementation details  LungGPT integrated with hospital information systems (HIS) via a secure application programming interface (API), compliant with data privacy regulations. Clinicians could access a web-based dashboard, input a patient’s identifier to retrieve structured (demographics, medical history) and unstructured (radiology reports, progress notes) data, with support for manual upload of additional lab results or imaging findings. Then LungGPT-Dx generated a ranked list of respiratory diseases, and LungGPT-Ex produced diagnostic rationales and treatment recommendations using a vectorized knowledge base of clinical guidelines. Outputs were reviewed by clinicians, who retained final decision-making authority, with options to adjust suggestions based on bedside observations. The interface underwent iterative usability testing by participating clinicians. Feedback from participating clinicians, including observations on usability and diagnostic alignment, informed iterative refinements to the interface and model outputs.     Quantification and statistical analysis  To evaluate the diagnostic performance of LungGPT, metrics such as AUC, the top-1/3 ACC, PRE, REC, and the F1 score were adopted. 95% confidence intervals for AUCs were estimated using the DeLong method. To evaluate the quality of the diagnostic explanations and treatment planning generated by LungGPT, three clinicians independently assessed outputs by using a 3-point Likert scale across three distinct dimensions (correctness, completeness, and truthfulness). To compare the clinical scores quantitatively, statistical analyses were performed using the Friedman test followed by Dunn’s multiple comparisons test. All the statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 26.0), where ∗ indicating  p  < 0.05, ∗∗ indicating  p  < 0.01, and ∗∗∗ indicating  p  < 0.001. evidence_text: NeoNet: A Novel Deep Learning Model for Retinal Disease Diagnosis and Localization. Retinal diseases are among the leading causes of vision impairment worldwide, and early detection is essential for enabling personalized treatments and preventing irreversible vision loss. In this paper, we propose a method aimed to identify and localize retinal conditions, i.e., Age-Related Macular Degeneration, Diabetic Retinopathy, and Choroidal Neovascularization, using explainable deep learning. For this purpose, we consider seven fine-tuned convolutional neural networks: MobileNet, LeNet, StandardCNN, CustomCNN, DenseNet, Inception, and EfficientNet. Moreover, we develop a novel architecture i.e., NeoNet, specifically designed for the detection of retinal diseases, achieving an accuracy of 99.5%. Furthermore, with the aim to provide explaianability behind the model decision, we highlight the most critical regions within retinal images influencing the predictions of the model. The obtained results show the ability of the model to detect pathological features, thereby supporting earlier and more accurate diagnosis of retinal diseases. 1. Introduction Retinal diseases, particularly Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD), Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), and Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV), represent some of the leading causes of visual impairment worldwide [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. Their incidence is progressively increasing, especially in older age groups and in individuals with previous diseases (e.g., diabetes) [ 4 ]. Therefore, their impact is significant, highlighting the importance of developing strategies for early detection of these diseases [ 5 ]. The retina is a highly specialized tissue of the central nervous system and is responsible for converting light signals into nerve impulses. Structurally, it is composed of ten layers extending from the retinal pigment epithelium to the inner limiting membrane. The retina acts as a neural processor, integrating and modulating visual information through the interaction between neuronal and glial cells, thus ensuring accurate visual perception adapted to environmental conditions [ 6 ]. The macula accounts for less than 5% of the total retinal surface area and is a specialized area located in the center of the visual axis responsible for central vision. At the center of the macula is the fovea, an area composed exclusively of cones, which provides visual acuity and color perception. This region is devoid of vasculature, which helps reduce light scattering, thus improving visual image quality. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have shown progress in the field of medical diagnostics as in retinal disease. Deep learning models, especially Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have achieved high accuracy in identifying retinal abnormalities and specific pathological signs, often reaching performance levels comparable to expert clinicians [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ]. A major limitation of these systems is the lack of explainability because most models operate as “black boxes” without providing insights into the reasoning behind their predictions, and this can impede clinical adoption, as ophthalmologists require interpretable evidence to validate and trust automated diagnostic decisions [ 7 , 11 , 12 , 13 ]. Starting from these considerations, this paper proposes an explainable method aimed at detecting and localizing a set of different retinal diseases, including AMD, DR, and CNV. In particular, AMD is a degenerative disease of the macula and one of the leading causes of blindness in adults over 65 years of age in Western countries. Globally, it affects more than 50% of individuals aged 80 and older [ 14 ]. AMD can evolve into two severe forms: the atrophic form and the exudative form. In the atrophic form, there is atrophy and thinning of the retinal pigment epithelium and surrounding structures, leading to loss of central vision. In the exudative form, on the other hand, there is the formation of abnormal blood vessels under the retina, which can cause fluid accumulation and hemorrhage, severely impairing vision. In this case, damage to the retina is more rapid and significant. Currently, there are no curative treatments but only therapeutic options aimed at slowing its progression, such as the use of vitamin and mineral supplements to manage symptoms of the atrophic form and reduce inflammation. In the case of the exudative form, however, they currently aim to block the growth of abnormal blood vessels under the retina through intravitreal injections of vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) inhibitors [ 14 ]. DR, instead, is a microangiopathy caused by the chronic effects of diabetes mellitus and is the most common retinal vascular disease. It affects about three out of four people 15 years after the development of diabetes and is the fifth leading cause of preventable blindness globally [ 15 ]. DR is divided into two main stages: nonproliferative retinopathy (NPDR) and proliferative retinopathy (PDR) [ 16 ]. In the NPDR stage, typical signs include microaneurysms and retinal hemorrhages [ 17 ]. In more advanced stages, PDR is characterized by the formation of new abnormal blood vessels (neovascularization) that develop on the optic nerve head or elsewhere on the retina, leading to complications [ 18 ]. Treatment of diabetic retinopathy focuses mainly on blood sugar control, but early diagnosis and regular monitoring are key to preventing blindness in patients with diabetic retinopathy. As a matter of fact, regular retinal screening programs and the use of advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence for retinal image analysis are improving the effectiveness of diagnosis and reducing cases of visual loss among diabetic patients [ 19 , 20 ]. Other possible treatments are laser photocoagulation, intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF to counteract neovascularization, and vitrectomy to treat cases of vitreal hemorrhage or retinal detachment traction. Finally, CNV is a complication of pathologic myopia characterized by the abnormal growth of new blood vessels from the choroid under the retina, leading to significant damage to vision [ 3 ]. It occurs mainly in myopic patients, with a more pronounced impact on women. Also for the treatment of myopic CNV is the use of anti-VEGF, which inhibits the growth of abnormal blood vessels, as well as photodynamic therapy (PDT), which allows selective destruction of neovases, minimizing damage to the surrounding retina. For the diagnosis of the three retinal diseases, we considered Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images. OCT is a non-invasive imaging modality based on the measurement of the echo time delay and intensity of backscattered light from different retinal layers. OCT is used to visualize the retinal layers in detail to assess the presence of signs of the disease and monitor the evolution and effectiveness of treatments. As a matter of fact, OCT produces cross-sectional images of the retina, enabling the visualization of structural alterations of the retina [ 21 ]. Furthermore, OCT provides retinal thickness and shows layer integrity and presence of fluid, important for staging and monitoring disease [ 22 ]. From a clinical perspective, each retinal disease is associated with specific OCT manifestations. In the case of AMD, OCT shows the presence of subretinal fluid or accumulation of drusen (deposits of lipid material between the retinal pigmented reticulum and Bruch’s membrane) [ 23 ]. In the case of DR, OCT allows significant thinning of the inner retinal layers to be noted, which is a sign of the disease [ 2 ]. In the advanced form of DR, hemorrhage and vascular abnormalities can be observed. In the case of CNV, OCT allows observation of retinal pigment epithelium lifting due to the presence of the underlying abnormal vessels and accumulation of fluid under the neurosensory retina, indicating neovascular activity [ 24 ]. In addition, through OCT angiography (OCT-A), there is direct visualization of the network of new blood vessels, highlighting their extent and location, useful in monitoring disease progression. Thus, early identification of these pathologies could play a crucial role in slowing or preventing visual deterioration, enabling more targeted and effective therapeutic interventions. In this paper, through the use of OCT images, we propose a series of CNNs, one designed and developed by the authors, i.e., NeoNet , to enable the automatic classification of retinal diseases. The proposed method takes into account also explainability; as a matter of fact, to introduce a rationale behind the decision of the model, we resort to the Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping technique (Grad-CAM), aimed to highlight the areas of the OCT of interest for the model prediction (and thus to localize the disease): in this way, we aim to increase transparency and trust in clinical practice [ 7 , 12 , 25 ]. This paper proceeds as follows: in the next section, the proposed method for explainable retinal disease detection and localization is presented; in Section 3 , the experimental analysis is described, accompanied by the obtained results; subsequently, the state-of-the-art comparison is discussed in Section 6 ; and, finally, conclusions and future work are reported in the last section. 2. The Method In this section, we introduce the proposed method designed to automatically detect and localize different retinal pathologies, i.e., AMD, DR, and CNV, and normal (in case of healthy retina). As illustrated in Figure 1 , the workflow of the proposed method consists of three main phases, described below in detail. Figure 1 The workflow of the proposed method, illustrating the main phases: training of pre-existing models, design of a new CNN architecture called NeoNet , and fine-tuning to improve performance in classifying retinal OCT images. Following the selection of the dataset, the first step of the proposed method involved training several pre-existing CNNs in order to evaluate their performance in classifying retinal images and to generate explainability using Grad-CAM. The second step involved the design and development of a new network, i.e., NeoNet , specifically designed for retinal disease classification. With the NeoNet model, we conduct experiments, generate the Grad-CAM visualizations, and we analyze the resulting outcomes. In the last step of the proposed method, fine-tuning was performed on the networks that had previously demonstrated the most interesting performance, with the consequent generation of the Grad-CAMs to evaluate the influence of fine-tuning on the results in terms of disease localization. 2.1. The CNN Models In the first phase of the proposed method shown in Figure 1 , several state-of-the-art CNNs were selected to set an initial performance benchmark. The analysis involved the evaluation of several well-known architectures, as detailed below: MobileNet: designed for lightweight models on mobile and embedded devices, uses depthwise separable convolutions to significantly reduce computation while maintaining performance; LeNet: provides a simple and effective foundation for understanding convolutional networks; StandardCNN: a CNN developed by the authors of [ 26 , 27 ], implemented for comparative purposes, consisting of a straightforward sequence of convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers; CustomCNN: another tailored CNN designed by the authors for comparative purposes; DenseNet: utilizes dense connectivity, where each layer receives inputs from all preceding layers, promoting feature reuse and alleviating the vanishing gradient problem; Inception: introduces parallel convolutional filters of different sizes within the same layer, allowing the network to capture features at multiple scales efficiently; EfficientNet: employs a compound scaling method that uniformly scales depth, width, and resolution, achieving high accuracy with fewer parameters and lower computational cost. Each model was tested with different learning rates and batch sizes, providing a detailed overview of evaluation metrics, such as loss, accuracy, precision, and recall. The new CNN architecture, called NeoNet, was designed motivated by the need to create a model capable of capturing relevant patterns in OCT images. In Figure 2 , the layer diagram of the NeoNet model is shown. The implementation of the proposed models is freely available for research purposes at the following url: https://mega.nz/file/tVkWSQDA#t6M_bUidSmrjdvlIyZwJ9foR02POMVpYgYlhcrzkXTo (accessed on 28 September 2025). Figure 2 NeoNet CNN layer diagram, developed for the analysis of retinal OCT images. As shown in Figure 2 , the NeoNet architecture consists of a sequence of five convolutional blocks, each made up of a 3 × 3 convolution with ReLU activation, followed by batch normalization and 2 × 2 max pooling. The number of filters in each block progressively increases (32, 64, 128, 256, 512), allowing the model to learn increasingly complex features. At the end of the convolutional phase, the feature maps were flattened through a Flatten layer and passed through two fully connected layers with 512 and 256 neurons, respectively, both regularized through 50% dropout. Finally, the output was obtained through a softmax layer, returning the probability of belonging to each class provided by the model. The NeoNet architecture was conceived with the aim of combining high classification accuracy with computational efficiency, which is particularly relevant for integration into real-time clinical workflows. NeoNet has a progressive increase in the number of filters across convolutional blocks (32–512) to effectively capture both low-level and high-level retinal features while avoiding excessive parameter growth. The inclusion of Batch Normalization and dropout layers further improves convergence stability and mitigates overfitting, enabling robust training on a moderately sized OCT dataset. Moreover, NeoNet was specifically tailored to balance model depth and width, reducing redundancy in feature extraction and ensuring a lightweight design compared to more complex architectures. 2.2. Grad-CAM To increase the explainability of the developed models, an analysis related to the prediction of the models was implemented through the Grad-CAM technique. This approach enabled the visualization of the regions within the input retinal images that most strongly influenced the model’s predictions, providing an intuitive understanding of the decision-making process. The qualitative analysis of Grad-CAMs allowed the evaluation of whether the major activation areas coincided with clinically relevant retinal structures, such as drusen, subretinal fluids, or vascular abnormalities, crucial elements in AMD, DR, and CNV diagnosis. In addition, the comparison of activations between the models enabled the observation of how custom training and fine-tuning influenced model-focusing capabilities. 3. Experimental Analysis In this section, we present the experimental analysis results, aimed to show the effectiveness of the proposed method. 3.1. Dataset To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method in the detection and localization of retinal disease, we resort to a real-world dataset composed of different retinal diseases and healthy retinas, i.e., the Retinal OCT-C8 dataset (Obuli Sai Naren. (2021) [ 28 ]). Retinal OCT-C8 is a public dataset composed of OCT images divided into 8 classes, totaling 24,000 images obtained after data augmentation techniques such as rotation, cropping, horizontal reflection, and contrast enhancement. The images are all in JPEG format but vary in size. In Table 1 , the distribution of images for each class is shown. The rows highlighted in blue are used to develop the CNN presented in this paper and subsequently for training the pre-existing models. Table 1 Distribution of retinal images across the original OCT-C8 dataset. The classes used in this work are highlighted in blue. Class Description Train Validate Test Total AMD Age-related Macular Degeneration 2300 350 350 3000 CNV Choroidal Neovascularization 2300 350 350 3000 CSR Central Serous Retinopathy 2300 350 350 3000 DME Diabetic Macular Edema 2300 350 350 3000 DR Diabetic Retinopathy 2300 350 350 3000 DRUSEN Yellow deposits under the retina 2300 350 350 3000 MH Macular Hole 2300 350 350 3000 NORMAL Healthy eyes with no abnormalities 2300 350 350 3000 Total 18,400 2800 2800 24,000 As already said, the original OCT-C8 dataset comprises 24,000 images. However, by selecting only the class of our interest, the size of the dataset has become 12,000 images, as shown in Table 2 that describes the dataset used in this work. Table 2 Distribution of eye images across the dataset used for the development of the CNN in this work. Class Train Validate Test Total AMD 2300 350 350 3000 CNV 2300 350 350 3000 DR 2300 350 350 3000 NORMAL 2300 350 350 3000 Total 9200 1400 1400 12,000 The dataset was divided into three subsets for the training, validation, and testing processes. The training set comprises approximately 75% of the total images, corresponding to 9200 images, and is used to train the machine learning models. The validation set contains 1400 images, which is ≃10% of the dataset and is employed to monitor the model during the training process to avoid overfitting and ensure the model is generalizing correctly. Finally, the test set, also consisting of 1400 images, is used to test and evaluate the final performance of the model. OCT images of the retina are essential for detailed observation of retinal morphology and abnormalities that characterize ocular diseases, as shown in Figure 3 . All the OCT images were resized to 224 × 224. Figure 3 Variants of OCT images within the dataset: ( A ) Normal, ( B ) AMD, ( C ) DR, and ( D ) CNV. In particular, Figure 3 A shows how a normal healthy retina appears as a series of distinct and uniform layers, alternating light and dark bands representing the different retinal structures. The foveal profile is symmetric and centered, with a slight depression in the center. In Figure 3 B, the normal foveal contour is disrupted, with subretinal and intraretinal fluid accumulation, as well as the presence of hyperreflective material beneath the retina indicative of AMD. DR may show thickening of the retina due to fluid accumulation, and hard deposits may be present within the retina as shown in Figure 3 C. In Figure 3 D, there is irregular uplift of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the macula, indicative of neovascular tissue and new vessel activity, with detachment of the RPE from Bruch’s membrane, typical of CNV. 3.2. Experimental Setup To implement the state-of-the-art CNN models and the NeoNet architecture, we used the TensorFlow library for Python 3.9 [ 29 ]. We consider the adoption of pre-existing architectures as baselines and the development of a custom model called NeoNet, designed specifically for the classification of retinal diseases. The training of all models, including NeoNet, was performed using the Retinal OCT-C8 subset exclusively, made up of four selected classes. The OCT-C8 dataset had already undergone several preprocessing operations before being released, including augmentation techniques such as cropping, padding, and horizontal flipping to increase variability and reduce overfitting. The augmented images were used exclusively for the training set, while validation and testing relied only on non-augmented data. In addition to resizing to 224 × 224 , the authors did not apply any further pre-processing steps. Hyperparameter optimization was performed via grid search to identify the optimal configuration for each CNN model, focusing on learning rate and batch size. The learning rate was tested at 0.001 and 0.0001 on a decreasing logarithmic scale to balance convergence speed and training stability. Batch size was evaluated at 16 and 32, balancing gradient stability and computational efficiency. Optimal hyperparameters were selected based on validation set accuracy, monitored over 50 epochs for each combination. Results indicated that high learning rates degraded performance, whereas conservative values were more effective. Increasing batch size from 16 to 32 generally improved performance, suggesting that greater gradient stability facilitates learning in OCT retinal image classification. Quantitative metrics commonly used in multiclass classification were employed to evaluate model performance. Model evaluation considered both validation loss, which quantifies the discrepancy between predicted and true labels, and accuracy as primary indicators. Additionally, precision quantifies the proportion of correctly predicted instances for a specific retinal class: (1) P r e c i s i o n = T P T P + F P where TP (true positives) denotes images correctly classified for a pathological condition (AMD, DR, CNV) and FP (false positives) those incorrectly assigned to the same class. Recall measures the model’s ability to identify all instances of a retinal disease in the dataset: (2) R e c a l l = T P T P + F N where FN (false negatives) represents images of a pathological class misclassified. Accuracy represents the overall proportion of correctly classified images: (3) A c c u r a c y = T P + T N T P + T N + F P + F N where TN (true negatives) are images correctly excluded from the class. The F-Measure assesses the balance between precision and recall: (4) F - M e a s u r e = 2 × P r e c i s i o n × R e c a l l P r e c i s i o n + R e c a l l The Area Under the Curve (AUC) measures the model’s ability to discriminate between classes. AUC values close to 1 indicate excellent performance, while values around 0.5 reflect random classification. 3.2.1. State-of-the-Art CNNs Along the development of NeoNet, some of the most popular state-of-the-art CNN architectures, including MobileNet, EfficientNet, and DenseNet, were adopted and trained in order to have a baseline to compare our results to. These models, already well established in the literature for their effectiveness in generic image classification, were selected for their ability to balance accuracy and computational complexity. This step allowed us to quickly evaluate the ability of the pre-existing models to distinguish between healthy retinas and pathological conditions, providing an initial benchmark for the performance achievable without full training from scratch. 3.2.2. Fine-Tuning of MobileNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet A fine-tuning procedure was implemented on three pre-trained models. Specifically, MobileNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet were selected to be readapted to the specific domain of OCT retinal images. Fine-tuning was performed by freezing the initial convolutional layers of each model, responsible for low-level features, and unfreezing deeper layers, more sensitive to complex features. After extracting the feature maps from the pre-trained base, new convolutional layers were added, followed by normalization and max pooling, and then two fully connected layers with 256 and 128 neurons, respectively, using ReLU activation and 50% dropout. The final layer uses a softmax activation function for the classification into the four target classes. This procedure was adopted with the aim of specializing pre-trained models, preserving the knowledge acquired during ImageNet training and adapting it to the specific context of retinal images. Fine-Tuning of MobileNet MobileNet is one of the models used for fine-tuning that takes advantage of the pre-trained architecture on ImageNet. The architecture uses MobileNet’s pre-trained convolutional layers, initially kept frozen to preserve the information acquired during training on a large generic dataset. Then, from the output of the base model, a new processing path is introduced that includes a convolutional layer with 64 3 × 3 filters and ReLU activation, followed by batch normalization to stabilize activations and improve convergence. To reduce the spatial dimensionality of the feature maps and retain the most relevant information, a ma pooling layer with a 2 × 2 window is employed. After this convolutional stage, a Flatten layer transforms the data into a one-dimensional vector, which is then processed by two fully connected layers with 256 and 128 units, both equipped with ReLU activation. To limit the risk of overfitting, a 50% dropout is applied to both. The output layer uses a softmax function, which generates a probability distribution among the classes in the dataset. During fine-tuning, the model adopts a strategy of progressively unlocking the layers, allowing the weights to be updated from the “conv_dw_11” layer of MobileNet. This approach allows selective adaptation of the representations without compromising the general features extracted from the initial convolutional layers. Figure 4 shows the architecture of the MobileNet with fine-tuning. Figure 4 Layer diagram for the fine-tuning of the MobileNet model. Fine-Tuning of EfficientNetB0 In the case of EfficientNetFT, the model uses EfficientNetB0 as a pre-trained network on ImageNet for feature extraction. Compared with the MobileNet-based version, a Conv2D layer with 64 filters and ReLU activation is added before the pooling phase, followed by batch normalization to stabilize learning. The phase of unlocking the weights for fine-tuning is set from block “block6”, allowing deeper layers of the network to be updated during training. In Figure 5 , there is the layer diagram of the new architecture. Figure 5 Layer diagram for the fine-tuning of the EfficientNetB0 model. Fine-Tuning of DenseNet For fine-tuning the DenseNet model, the DenseNet121 model is used for feature extraction, again with pre-trained weights. Compared to the EfficientNetFT version, no additional convolutional layers are added: the first layer of the custom head is directly a MaxPooling2D, followed by two fully connected layers with 50% dropout to reduce the risk of overfitting. Fine-tuning is enabled from the “conv5_block3” block, allowing the high-level features of the network to be updated. In Figure 6 , there is the layer diagram of the fine-tuned architecture. Results of State-of-the-Art CNN Architectures Compared to other convolutional neural networks evaluated on the same Retinal OCT-C8 dataset, NeoNet stands out with remarkably high accuracy. However, several well-established models achieved similarly competitive results. Notably, EfficientNet reached the highest overall performance, achieving up to 99.90% accuracy, precision, and recall with a loss of just 0.025. Similarly, MobileNet achieved strong results, with a maximum accuracy of 99.85%, confirming its lightweight yet effective architecture. DenseNet and Inception also demonstrated excellent performance, both exceeding 99.70% accuracy under optimal hyperparameter settings. In contrast, Standard CNN reached a peak accuracy of 98.50%, showing solid but slightly inferior performance. At the lower end, LeNet exhibited a substantial performance gap, with a maximum accuracy of only 35.00%, underscoring limitations in capturing the complex feature representations required for this dataset. When directly compared to a specific architecture such as Custom CNN, NeoNet maintains a performance edge, achieving slightly higher accuracy. For example, Custom CNN attained a best accuracy of 97.50% with a corresponding loss of 0.160, while NeoNet surpassed this in all tested configurations. Nevertheless, Custom CNN displayed notable training stability, with consistent accuracy trends and lower loss fluctuations across epochs. This robustness suggests that Custom CNN is less sensitive to variations in hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size, making it a viable alternative when computational simplicity and training stability are prioritized. Importantly, all networks were trained from scratch on the selected OCT-C8 subset, ensuring a fair comparison under identical conditions. When analyzing the number of trainable parameters, it is evident that lightweight architectures such as MobileNet (3.4M parameters) and EfficientNet (5.5M) achieve accuracy comparable to much heavier models like Inception (23.8M) or Standard CNN (44.5M). This highlights that model efficiency, rather than parameter count alone, plays a crucial role in performance on OCT images. In this regard, NeoNet was specifically designed to provide a favorable trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, achieving competitive results with a more balanced parameter footprint. Results After Fine-Tuning of MobileNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet During training, all three models showed progressive improvement in loss and accuracy. MobileNet showed consistent improvement throughout the training process. The training loss steadily decreased from an initial value of 0.40 in the first epoch to near zero in the final iterations, indicating that the model effectively learned the distinctive features of each class. Training accuracy increased progressively, reaching 100% in the final epoch. Precision and recall remained high throughout training, suggesting reliable classification across all classes. On the test set, MobileNet achieved a loss of 0.020, with an accuracy of 99.71%, precision of 99.91%, and recall of 99.71%, demonstrating excellent generalization and robust performance. High precision indicates that the model minimizes false positives, while high recall shows effective identification of images belonging to each class. Maintaining these metrics at high levels throughout training highlights the model’s reliability in distinguishing between various pathological conditions and normal cases. The results obtained from the EfficientNetFT and DenseNetFT models also demonstrate significant performance, with notable differences in terms of accuracy and generalization ability. EfficientNetFT achieved a strong performance during training, reaching a final training accuracy of 93.45%, with a precision of 89.25% and a recall of 91.23%. The training loss decreased steadily from 1.331 at epoch 0 to 0.125 at epoch 50, indicating effective learning. On the test set, the model achieved a final accuracy of 70.14%, with a precision of 71.88% and a recall of 69.21%. The F1-score reached 70.52%, while the AUC was 88.73%, indicating a good ability to distinguish between classes. However, per-class analysis revealed critical issues, particularly for the DR class, which had a very low recall (24.86%) despite high precision (98.86%). The other classes, AMD and NORMAL, showed better performance, with accuracy of 95.64% and 88.50%, and AUCs of 95.38% and 79.67%, respectively. During training, DenseNetFT showed rapid convergence and excellent learning capability, achieving a final training accuracy of 99.96%, with a precision of 99.97% and a recall of 99.96%. The training loss decreased from 0.278 at epoch 0 to 0.0008 at epoch 50. On the test set, DenseNetFT demonstrated significantly superior performance, with an accuracy of 98.50%, precision of 98.60%, and recall of 98.40%. The F1-score reached 98.50%, and the AUC was 99.80%, indicating excellent generalization capability. In particular, for the DR class, recall improved dramatically, reaching 97.50%, compared to the 24.86% obtained with EfficientNetFT. The other classes also achieved excellent performance, with accuracy above 97% and AUC values close to 1.0000. While EfficientNetFT delivered acceptable results, DenseNetFT stands out for its significantly higher accuracy and robustness, especially in classifying more complex cases such as DR. This advantage may be attributed to DenseNet’s greater architectural complexity, which allows it to extract more discriminative features from the dataset. Related Work In this section, we review the current state of the art in the detection of ocular pathologies by exploiting deep learning. This overview is intended to support researchers working on retinal disease detection by providing a structured and accessible summary of current challenges, recent methodological advances, and future perspectives in the deep learning-based detection of AMD, DR, and CNV. As a matter of fact, there are several papers aimed to detect ocular diseases; for instance, the one proposed by Tariqul Islam et al. [ 30 ] achieved interesting results in terms of F-score and AUC, where the authors consider a pre-processing step using the CLAHE algorithm to enhance image quality, followed by data augmentation. A CNN was employed for multiclass classification of several ocular diseases. Kuldeep Vayadande et al. [ 31 ] compare several models, i.e., VGG19 and Inception V3, with VGG19 emerging as the most effective for ocular disease detection. Their findings highlight the importance of architecture selection in optimizing classification accuracy. Authors in [ 32 ] achieved 99.7% accuracy. Additionally, they applied attention maps for explainability. Unlike Grad-CAM heatmaps, attention maps are integrated during training to enhance performance, which introduces additional computational complexity and potential interpretability challenges. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as Grad-CAM have become increasingly important in retinal image analysis to improve model transparency and clinical trust. Grad-CAM, introduced by Selvaraju et al. [ 33 ], enables visualization of the image regions that most influence model predictions, aiding clinical interpretation. Other studies, including Schlemper et al. [ 34 ], have employed attention maps and saliency methods to explain convolutional neural networks in ocular disease detection, underscoring the crucial role of XAI for validation and adoption of AI systems in medical practice. In 2023, Keya Wang et al. [ 35 ] presented MbsaNet, combining CNNs with self-attention. Though their preprocessing (resizing to 224 × 224 and data augmentation) mirrors ours, the accuracy under multiclass classification was lower. In recent years, several large-scale foundation models have emerged for OCT-based retinal disease modeling, demonstrating impressive performance in both diagnostic and prognostic tasks. Among them, RETFound [ 9 ] represents a transformer-based model pre-trained in a self-supervised manner on more than 1.6 million unlabeled retinal images (OCT and fundus). This approach has proven effective across multiple downstream tasks, including disease classification and progression prediction. Similarly, VisionFM [ 36 ], a multimodal foundation model trained on over 3.4 million imaging exams, has shown expert-level performance in diagnostic settings by integrating fundus, OCT, and other modalities. EyeFound [ 37 ], although still under active development, aims to extend this approach further by unifying retinal imaging modalities through an end-to-end foundation architecture. More recently, OCTCube-M [ 38 ] introduced a hybrid 3D masked autoencoder and multimodal architecture specifically designed to handle the volumetric nature of OCT scans, significantly improving performance in cross-device and systemic diagnostic tasks. Finally, MIRAGE [ 39 ] proposes a flexible multimodal foundation model capable of performing both classification and segmentation tasks across OCT and scanning laser ophthalmoscopy data, exhibiting high generalization ability and robustness to unseen data distributions. As shown in Table 6 , the main difference with respect to the state of the art and the proposed method lies in the introduction of a novel deep learning architecture specifically designed and developed by the authors. This is further enhanced by the integration of explainability, indicated by the checkmark symbol in the table, through the Grad-CAM technique, which enables qualitative assessment of the model’s focus on clinically relevant retinal features, thereby increasing the transparency and potential clinical trustworthiness of the system.
