Retained cell type/cluster label proportions at 0.10 sketching fraction for ( A ) Merfish mouse ovary; ( B ) Merfish sagittal mouse brain; ( C ) Xenium human breast cancer; ( D ) Xenium human lung; ( E ) Xenium whole mouse pup; ( F ) Visium HD coronal mouse brain; ( G ) Visium HD mouse embryo; ( H ) Visium HD ovarian cancer.            For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.         In contrast, the largest shifts in label proportions arose when comparing leverage-score-based methods to transcriptome-driven geometric sketching. Spatial smoothing of the input data produced only modest changes within the same methodological family (e.g. leverage score versus spatially smoothed leverage score), consistent with smoothing acting primarily as a stabilizer rather than altering the sampling objective. Across datasets, leverage-score approaches generally maintained label proportions more faithfully, whereas geometric sketching on expression features (scSampler/geoSketch on RNA) sometimes substantially distorted proportions, particularly in the Visium HD and whole mouse pup datasets (Fig.  4E – H ). For example, in the Visium HD ovarian cancer dataset, the Fibroblast CAF population increased from roughly 20% of the full dataset to over 70% of cells in the scSampler and geoSketch RNA sketches (Fig.  4H ). A plausible explanation is that this population exhibits high transcriptional heterogeneity, causing geometric sketching methods to preferentially sample it to achieve coverage of the expression manifold. While such behavior may be desirable when the goal is to capture transcriptomic diversity, it can bias downstream analyses that rely on representative cell-type composition (e.g. estimates of cell-type abundance, comparisons of compositional changes across conditions, and niche frequency quantification).  These results emphasize that sketch selection should be guided by the intended downstream task. If preserving approximate cell-type proportions in the sketched dataset is important—and particularly if labels inferred from the sketch will be interpreted directly without being projected back to the full dataset—then leverage-based approaches provide a more conservative choice (Fig.  4 ). Conversely, if the primary objective is to capture rare transcriptional states or highly variable populations, transcriptome-driven geometric sketching may still be warranted, with the caveat that the resulting sketches may not be compositionally representative. Given that both leverage-based and geometric sketching methods are relatively fast to run, we recommend applying both in parallel for cell-type discovery and then projecting sketch-derived labels back onto the full dataset to reconcile differences and evaluate robustness, since accurate cell-type annotation is foundational to most ST workflows.    Hausdorff distances  At a fixed 10% sampling fraction, we compared sketch quality using robust (partial) Hausdorff distance computed in both transcriptomic space and physical coordinate space (Fig.  5 ). In transcriptomic space, differences between sketching strategies were modest across datasets: for any given dataset, the total spread in Hausdorff distances across methods was typically small (on the order of 1 unit or less), indicating broadly comparable coverage of the expression manifold at this sampling rate. Consequently, although Fig.  5A  visualizes method-to-method differences, the absolute magnitude of separation is limited at 10% sampling. Consistent with this observation, larger divergences between algorithms became more apparent only at higher sampling fractions, as shown in the extended data figures reporting performance across sampling fractions (Extended data Figs 5–12, top panel). Because many practical applications of sketching in ST involve stronger downsampling than 50%, we emphasize that at commonly used low sampling fractions, transcriptomic Hausdorff distance alone is unlikely to provide a decisive criterion for choosing between leverage-based and geometric sketching approaches. In contrast, coordinate-space Hausdorff distance revealed substantially larger performance differences and more clearly separated the methods (Fig.  5B ). As expected, coordinate-based sketching produced the smallest coordinate Hausdorff distances due to explicitly optimizing spatial coverage; however, this objective does not necessarily align with preserving transcriptomic structure. Among transcriptome-informed methods, leverage-based approaches consistently achieved lower coordinate Hausdorff distances than geometric sketching methods across all Visium HD datasets, indicating improved spatial coverage of the tissue while still selecting points based on molecular structure. No dataset showed a clear coordinate-space advantage for geometric sketching, although the sagittal mouse brain and human lung datasets exhibited broadly similar performance across methods (Fig.  5B ; Extended data Figs 5–12, second panel). Together, these results suggest that when spatial coverage is a priority, particularly in highly structured tissues, in samples with large variability in local cell density, or in settings where spatial organization and transcriptional heterogeneity are confounded, leverage-based sketching provides a robust default for minimizing spatial “holes” while maintaining comparable transcriptomic coverage.    Cluster concordance and spatial domain conservation  To investigate how sketching impacts downstream spatial analyses, we evaluated preservation of spatial domain structure by identifying tissue domains in the full and sketched datasets and quantifying concordance between them (Fig.  6 ). Spatial domains were inferred using the Randimized spatial PCA (RASP) workflow [ 33 ] (PCA-based smoothing followed by clustering) under two parameterizations chosen to capture either smaller, finer-grained niches (Fig.  6A ) or larger, coarser tissue compartments (Fig.  6B ; see Extended data Section 1.3.4 for details). For each dataset, we computed an ARI between the domain labels obtained from the sketch and those obtained from the corresponding full dataset. In parallel, we performed canonical graph-based clustering directly on each sketch (i.e. neighbor graph construction in transcriptomic space followed by community detection, as commonly used in standard single-cell and spatial transcriptomics pipelines for defining clusters prior to cell-type annotation) and computed the ARI against the corresponding full-data cell type or cluster labels (Extended data Figs 5–12, second panel from bottom). This complementary analysis serves a different purpose than the RASP-based spatial domain comparison: whereas RASP explicitly integrates spatial context via smoothing and is designed to recover contiguous tissue domains or niches, graph-based clustering measures whether sketching preserves the intrinsic transcriptomic neighborhood structure that underlies routine downstream analyses such as clustering, differential expression, and cell-type annotation. Because these two workflows emphasize different signal components, spatial compartments versus expression-driven community structure, agreement under both provides a more complete picture of sketch fidelity and helps distinguish methods that preserve spatial domains from those that primarily preserve transcriptomic clusters. At a 10% sampling fraction, leverage-score-based sketching methods generally preserved small spatial domains at least as well as, and often better than, geometric sketching approaches. In six out of eight datasets, leverage-based methods were comparable to or outperformed geometric methods in small-domain ARI, with the spatially smoothed leverage variant achieving the highest ARI among the four leverage-based strategies in the majority of cases (Fig.  6A ). In contrast, spatial smoothing applied prior to geometric sketching did not yield a consistent benefit: depending on the dataset, smoothing sometimes improved and sometimes reduced domain concordance, suggesting that its effects are context-dependent rather than uniformly stabilizing.  For larger spatial domains, leverage-based methods again tended to match or exceed geometric sketching performance (seven of eight datasets; Fig.  6B ), although we observed increased variability in ARI across repeated runs for many methods and datasets, indicating that at 10% sampling fraction the inferred domain solutions can be unstable. In some instances, spatial smoothing improved ARI (e.g. Visium HD brain and mouse ovary), but this trend was not consistent: in two datasets, smoothing reduced ARI for the leverage-based method, and only the ovarian cancer dataset showed a clear advantage for geometric sketching. Taken together, these results suggest that when spatial domain detection is a key downstream objective, leverage-based sketching provides a conservative default choice, a conclusion that is also reflected in the aggregated rank-sum comparisons (Fig.  3B ), which summarize domain-preservation performance across datasets and metrics.    Cell type spatial structure preservation  We evaluated preservation of global cell-type spatial structure by computing Moran’s I for each cell type (or cluster label) in both the full and sketched datasets, yielding a label-specific measure of spatial autocorrelation. For each label, we then quantified sketch-induced distortion as the log 2 FC between the Moran’s I value in the sketch and the corresponding value in the full dataset. Extended data Fig.  1  illustrates this procedure using representative spatial scatter plots for selected labels, alongside method-specific log 2 FC values. As expected, uniform sampling produced the smallest deviations from the full dataset for this metric, consistent with its lack of structure-dependent sampling bias.  We also provide complete cell-type-level results across all eight datasets in  Supplementary Figs S13  and  S14 , without applying minimum baseline autocorrelation filters. This comprehensive view reveals that signal in these metrics is primarily driven by cell types with inherently high baseline spatial autocorrelation—namely, those with strong intrinsic spatial organization in the full dataset. Cell types that are sparsely or uniformly distributed across the tissue exhibit low Moran’s I values regardless of sketching method, reflecting their dispersed spatial distribution rather than poor sketch quality. Indeed, for datasets containing many uniformly distributed cell types, Moran’s I values across sketching methods converge, suggesting limited meaningful variation to preserve for these populations. Consequently, spatial autocorrelation metrics are most informative for cell types with moderately to highly organized spatial structure; sparse populations should not be expected to show stable or differentiated Moran’s I signatures across methods.  Dataset-wide patterns across all labels are summarized in Extended data Fig.  2A  and  B , and  Supplementary Figs S13  and  S14 . To compare sketching methods systematically within each dataset, we ranked methods separately for every label by the absolute Moran’s I distortion (|log 2 FC|) assigning rank 1 to the method with the smallest absolute deviation (best preservation). We then summed ranks across all labels to obtain a dataset-level rank-sum for each method, reflecting overall preservation of label-specific spatial autocorrelation. Because the datasets contain different numbers of labels, raw rank-sums are not directly comparable across datasets; therefore, we standardized rank-sums within each dataset (row-wise) using both min–max scaling (Extended data Fig.  2A ) and  z -scoring (Extended data Fig.  2B ) and visualized the results as heatmaps. For interpretability, we omitted uniform sampling from these heatmaps because it was consistently the top performer and would otherwise compress differences among the remaining methods (see Extended data Section 1.3.5 for details).  Unlike metrics such as spatial coverage or domain preservation, Moran’s I distortion did not yield a single dominant ”best” method class across all datasets. However, the reduced-rank leverage variant (leverage svd) achieved the best (lowest) standardized rank-sum in four out of eight datasets and performed comparably to the best method in all but two. Notably, this was the only metric for which spatially smoothed geometric sketching (geoSketch) performed well in a substantial subset of datasets (three out of eight). The stronger performance of leverage svd relative to the full leverage score is plausible because the truncated SVD can act as a denoising step that emphasizes dominant, spatially coherent sources of variation while down-weighting high-frequency or sample-specific transcriptional noise; in turn, this may reduce the tendency to over-sample locally heterogeneous regions that can perturb global label autocorrelation. Additionally, operating in a reduced-rank subspace can stabilize the leverage signal in high-dimensional settings, making sampling less sensitive to idiosyncratic gene-level variance. Taken together, these results suggest that when preservation of global spatial autocorrelation of labels is important for downstream analyses, a reduced-rank leverage approach provides a robust default choice, particularly for cell types with intrinsic spatial organization.    Simulated dataset sketching results  This analysis consisted three Visium HD-like and three Xenium-like datasets with different patterns (complex, radial, and striped; see Extended data Fig.  3A  and  E ). For all six datasets, minimization of both transcriptomic Hausdorff distance was similar for all tested algorithms, across sampled fractions, with RNA-based scSampler performing the worst across all datasets, and leverage score performing best (Extended data Figs  3B  and  F , and  4A  and  E ). For comparison of coordinate-based Hausdorff distances, note that the Visium-like datasets are lacking coordinate-based sketching methods, as they are akin to uniform sampling in this context. For this metric, spatially smoothed Geosketch and scSampler performed the worst, while uniform and leverage score achieved the smallest Hausdorff distance for the Visium-like dataset, with coordinate-based Geosketch performing best on all the Xenium-like datasets (Extended data Figs  3C  and  G , and  4B  and  F ). However, for both Hausdorff distance comparisons across datasets and between algorithms, all algorithms do a good job minimizing the distance for both coordinates and transcriptomic space, as can been seen with the small variation in values across the sampling fractions. The ARI results show a divergence in algorithm performance across simulated datasets. For the Visium like datasets, there is some variability across sampling fractions, but leverage score and smoothed leverage score, followed by uniform sampling perform best, RNA and smoothed scSampler perform worst (Extended data Figs  3D  and  4C ). For the Xenium-like datasets, there is no clear best performing algorithm for the complex and radial datasets; however, scSampler variants still under-perform (Extended data Fig.  3H  and  G ). Notably, for both stripe datasets, leverage score and smoothed leverage score significantly outperform all other algorithms (Extended data Figs  3D  and  H , and  4G ).    Comprehensive spatial analysis vignette  This vignette, based on the Allen Institute MERFISH mouse brain dataset, illustrates that the downstream consequences of sketching depend not only on the sampling strategy itself, but also on the spatial structure and biological scale of the feature under consideration. Full analytical details, methods, and extended results are provided in the Supplementary Methods and accompanying vignette file (allen_vignette.html). Briefly, we found that the impact of sketching was heterogeneous across analysis types:    Globally organized or highly aggregated signals (for example, mean pathway activity scores) were generally well preserved across methods, with only modest differences between approaches. This likely reflects the redundancy inherent in such signals, which are supported by many genes or broad expression programs.    Spatially organized feature-level signals (including Moran’s I of individual genes, ligand–receptor interaction patterns, and spatially structured pathway or transcription factor activities) were substantially more sensitive to sampling strategy. In these settings, leverage-based approaches consistently outperformed density-agnostic geometric methods, whereas spatial smoothing provided only partial recovery of performance.    Weakly spatially organized signals (such as broadly distributed genes or relatively uniform pathway activities) showed more limited dependence on sketching method, with most approaches yielding similar results.    High-resolution spatial features (for example, transcription factor activity restricted to specific anatomical regions) were especially vulnerable to undersampling by nonspatially aware methods. In these cases, geometric sketches could substantially under-represent the very regions most relevant for biological interpretation.    Together, these results highlight a central practical point for STs analysis: the importance of sketching strategy increases with the spatial specificity of the biological question. For routine tasks such as general quality control, broad cell-type visualization, or coarse pathway summarization, most sketching approaches may be adequate. By contrast, for analyses aimed at identifying spatially resolved biological programs, leverage-based sampling, particularly when combined with spatial smoothing, more faithfully preserved the signals most relevant for downstream interpretation while still providing substantial reductions in dataset size.     Discussion  Our benchmarking across diverse ST platforms and tissues indicates that sketching method choice should be driven by the specific downstream quantities one aims to preserve, rather than by transcriptomic coverage alone. At commonly used sampling fractions (e.g. 10%), transcriptomic Hausdorff distance was consistently similar across methods, suggesting that most algorithms adequately capture broad expression-space coverage and that this metric is rarely decisive in practice (Fig.  3B , top row). In contrast, metrics that directly reflect structure and spatial coverage in coordinate space, preservation of spatial domains, and recovery of cluster labels—showed clearer separation: uniform sampling and leverage-based approaches generally outperformed transcriptome-driven geometric sketching methods across real datasets, with similar trends (albeit weaker) in simulated data (Fig.  3B  and  D ). The weaker separation observed on simulated benchmarks should not be interpreted as evidence that sketching objectives are inherently less distinct in controlled settings, but rather reflects limitations of current ST simulators in capturing the multiscale complexity of real tissues. In particular, SRTsim-style simulations typically operate over a reduced feature space and generate expression patterns with comparatively smooth, idealized spatial organization, fewer sharp anatomical boundaries, and less within–cell type heterogeneity than platform data. As a result, (i) transcriptome-driven manifold geometry is less informative for differentiating sketch objectives, and (ii) spatially informed heuristics (including smoothing) can align more closely with the simulation’s generative assumptions than with real tissues, which contain substantial technical variation (e.g. capture efficiency gradients, segmentation artifacts, ambient RNA) and biological microstructure that partially decouple spatial proximity from expression similarity. These considerations motivate using simulated benchmarks as complementary stress tests rather than as fully predictive surrogates for real-data performance, and further emphasize the importance of evaluating sketching methods on diverse experimental datasets.  These results reinforce a key practical point: when users care about spatially grounded analyses (e.g. domain detection, neighborhood statistics, spatial differential expression, or niche quantification), method selection should prioritize spatial fidelity metrics rather than minor differences in transcriptomic Hausdorff distance.  Consistent with this, we observed that transcriptome-driven geometric sketching (scSampler/geoSketch on expression features) can substantially distort compositional summaries when highly heterogeneous populations dominate the expression manifold. In several datasets, most strikingly the Visium HD ovarian cancer and whole mouse pup examples—geometric sketches altered cell-type proportions far more than leverage-based sketches (Fig.  4 ), likely because manifold-coverage objectives preferentially oversample transcriptionally variable regions. Such distortion can bias downstream interpretation when sketches are analyzed in isolation (e.g. apparent shifts in cell-type abundance, altered niche frequencies, or misleading comparisons across conditions). In contrast, leverage-based sampling more consistently preserved label proportions while still providing a transcriptome-informed subset. When the primary objective is to discover rare transcriptional states or characterize high-variance substructure, geometric sketching remains valuable, but we recommend projecting sketch-derived labels back onto the full dataset before making compositional claims. More broadly, running both a leverage-based and a geometric sketch in parallel and comparing projected annotations provides an efficient robustness check for cell typing and state discovery.  Among spatially informed metrics, coordinate-space Hausdorff distance and domain-preservation ARI most strongly favored leverage-based approaches. Coordinate-only sketching (used here primarily as a baseline) unsurpris-ingly optimized spatial coverage but is not broadly applicable across platforms (e.g. Visium HD’s regular grid) and can miss transcriptional extremes. Leverage-based sketches, by contrast, frequently achieved substantially better spatial coverage than geometric expression sketches—particularly in highly structured tissues or in samples with strong variability in local sampling density—while maintaining comparable transcriptomic coverage. Similarly, for spatial domain detection using RASP-derived small and large domain parameterizations, leverage-based methods were the conservative best choice in the majority of datasets, although domain solutions at 10% sampling exhibited nontrivial variance, emphasizing the need for repeated runs or stability checks. Finally, preservation of global label spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I) revealed a nuanced pattern: uniform sampling was consistently best, but among nonuniform methods, reduced-rank leverage (leverage svd) emerged as a robust choice across datasets, suggesting that truncated subspace sampling can better maintain global spatial label structure than full-rank leverage in some settings. Taken together, these results support the following practical guidance: use leverage-based sketching as a default when spatial coverage, clustering concordance, or domain detection are key; prefer reduced-rank leverage when preserving global spatial autocorrelation of labels is particularly important; and reserve transcriptome-driven geometric sketching for applications centered on capturing transcriptional heterogeneity and rare states, ideally coupled with label projection back to the full dataset for unbiased spatial and compositional interpretation.  It should be noted that several of the evaluation metrics used here can, in principle, be improved by post hoc heuristics that are not part of the underlying sketch objective, and we therefore interpret them as diagnostics of ’fixed-budget’ sketch fidelity rather than as adversarially robust measures. For example, starting from a coordinate-or uniform-based sketch and then augmenting it with spatial k-nearest neighbors of selected points could artificially improve label- and neighborhood-based metrics (e.g. ARI, Moran’s I, and domain concordance), and may also reduce coordinate-space Hausdorff distance, largely by increasing local redundancy. Such “completion” strategies, however, effectively change the sampling distribution and/or increase the information budget by trading breadth of coverage for nearby, correlated points, which can reduce the sketch’s ability to capture transcriptomic extremes and rare states under a fixed sampling fraction. In this regard, expression-space Hausdorff distance and PCA-structure preservation are comparatively less susceptible to purely spatial neighbor augmentation (and can even worsen as redundancy increases), whereas spatial label metrics are more vulnerable when labels are spatially smooth. Future work could explicitly study budget-matched two-stage baselines (e.g. coordinate sketch + neighbor completion with the same final sketch size), incorporate redundancy penalties or effective-sample-size measures, and adopt holdout-based task evaluations (e.g. generalization of clustering/domain assignments or neighborhood composition to withheld cells) to reduce opportunities for metric-driven “gaming” and to better align evaluation with downstream scientific use cases.  Looking forward, our findings motivate sketching frameworks that explicitly optimize joint objectives over transcriptomic and spatial fidelity while providing predictable behavior for compositional preservation. Promising directions include multi-objective sampling that balances expression-space coverage with coordinate-space coverage, adaptive strategies that account for local density variation, and stability-aware domain-preserving sketches. As ST datasets continue to scale in both cell count and complexity, such methods will be essential for enabling rapid exploratory analysis without inadvertently distorting the spatial and compositional signals that often motivate ST experiments in the first place. title: FineST: contrastive learning integrates histology and spatial transcriptomics for nuclei-resolved ligand-receptor analysis.
xenium_reason: Xenium is mentioned without evidence of dataset generation or reuse
evidence_text: FineST: contrastive learning integrates histology and spatial transcriptomics for nuclei-resolved ligand-receptor analysis. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing cell-cell communication (CCC) across various biological processes, ranging from embryonic development to cancer progression. However, its limited resolution and high data sparsity hinder the detailed characterization of CCC patterns within complex tissues. Here, we introduce FineST, a deep contrastive learning model that leverages a histology foundation model to fuse ST and histology images, enabling Fine-grained Spatial Transcriptomics analysis. This approach facilitates precise nuclei segmentation, high-resolution RNA expression imputation, and the identification of intricate ligand-receptor interactions. Using both colorectal cancer VisiumHD and breast cancer Xenium datasets, we demonstrate that FineST significantly outperforms existing methods in high-resolution RNA imputation, cell type prediction, and CCC pattern discovery. With focused application to the Visium platform, FineST reveals novel biological insights into tumor-immune interactions across multiple cancer types, including invasive fronts in breast cancer, tertiary lymphoid structures in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and PD-1 therapy resistance barriers in hepatocellular carcinoma. These findings highlight a new paradigm in ST analysis through the integration of readily available histology images.

evidence_text:
Single-cell spatial analysis identifies ID1-high endothelial cells in tertiary lymphoid structures as predictors of durable response to immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer. BACKGROUND: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) maturity and cellular composition shape resistance or sensitivity to immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) across cancers. Single-cell spatial resolution data for the endothelial compartment of TLSs are lacking; therefore, we investigated the cellular composition, endothelial dynamics, and cell-cell interactions within TLS regions. METHODS: We applied high-resolution Xenium In Situ spatial transcriptomics to eight samples collected from non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLC) (four after chemoimmunotherapy, four untreated), extracted 90 TLS regions, generated approximately 320,000 single-cell profiles from those regions, and analyzed the endothelial compartment within each TLS. We independently assessed the exploratory findings using multiplex immunofluorescence and survival analysis in a separate cohort of 45 patients receiving immunotherapy. RESULTS: Spatial mapping revealed a reproducible, B-cell-dominant TLS architecture across all samples. Mature TLSs contained CXCL13-rich follicular cores and were associated with a favorable prognosis. Within the endothelial compartment, high endothelial cells (HECs) forming high-endothelial venules (HEVs) segregated from other endothelial cells; in mature TLSs these HECs exhibited high inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1) expression and an adhesion molecular signature, promoting lymphocyte recruitment. Patients with tumors harboring ID1-high HEVs showed higher response rates and pronounced survival advantage; multivariable analysis confirmed ID1-high status as an independent prognostic factor. Conversely, ICB exposure eventually reduced ID1 expression and adhesion molecule levels in HECs, impaired lymphocyte trafficking, and promoted a shift toward a remodeled endothelial state. CONCLUSIONS: ID1expression, linked to HEC differentiation during TLS maturation or ICB exposure, marks a functionally mature, lymphocyte-recruiting HEV that predict durable response to immunotherapy. These findings provide a novel mechanistic framework and practical biomarkers for HEV-centered immuno-oncology strategies in NSCLC. Keywords:  Biomarker, CXCL12, High endothelial venules, ID1, Immunotherapy, Non-small-cell lung cancer, Remodeling, Spatial single-cell analysis, Spatial transcriptomics, Tertiary lymphoid structures      status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Received 2025 Aug 21; Accepted 2025 Dec 27; Collection date 2026.       Introduction  Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide [ 1 ]. Platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy combining cytotoxic agents with immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) has extended survival in some patients and is standard both as a neoadjuvant setting and a first-line treatment for advanced disease [ 2 – 5 ]. Despite ongoing real-world data analyses, reliable biomarkers capable of definitively distinguishing durable responders from non-responders are needed [ 6 ,  7 ].  The presence and maturity of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) within the tumor microenvironment have emerged as key prognostic and predictive elements across multiple solid tumors [ 8 – 10 ]. In NSCLC, the densities of DC-LAMP⁺ mature dendritic cells and CD20⁺ B cells within TLSs are correlated with long-term survival [ 11 ,  12 ]. Mature TLSs are linked to favorable ICI response in various types of cancers, such as NSCLC and bladder cancer, and then high levels of intra-tumoral CXCL13 expression mark patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer likely to respond to treatment [ 13 ,  14 ].  The canonical 12-chemokine “TLS gene signature” is employed to predict TLS regions in transcriptomic analyses [ 15 ,  16 ]. However, its expression varies across tumor types, underscoring the inter-cancer TLS heterogeneity and the need for more tumor-specific functional TLS markers [ 17 ]. Our re-analysis of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to isolate TLS-like cells with the 12-chemokine scores yielded few B-cell populations in breast ( n  = 26) and lung ( n  = 185) cancer samples (Supplementary Fig. S1A, B) [ 18 ,  19 ], highlighting the limitations of dissociative single-cell methods for analyzing structured niches. Therefore, spatially resolved transcriptomics is essential for capturing TLS architecture and heterogeneity in situ.  Previous studies have investigated spatial transcriptomics focused on TLS [ 20 – 22 ]. Immature TLSs enriched with immunosuppressive macrophages and regulatory T cells confer resistance to ICB, particularly in peritoneal metastases in gastric cancer [ 23 ]. Additionally, tumors containing mature TLSs can exhibit primary ICB resistance driven by distinct cancer-associated fibroblast subsets (FAP⁺ αSMA⁺ and MYH11⁺ αSMA⁺) in NSCLC [ 24 ]. Collectively, these studies demonstrated the effects of both TLS maturity and cellular composition on therapeutic outcomes. However, to date, the spatiotemporal dynamics of endothelial cells within TLSs have not been assessed using single-cell resolution methods.  Therefore, the present study applied high-resolution Xenium In Situ spatial single-cell transcriptomics to resected NSCLC specimens. We investigated the cellular components, endothelial cell dynamics, and cell–cell interactions within TLS associated region by TLS maturity and treatment status with or without chemo-immunotherapy. The study design is shown in Fig.  1 . The resulting dataset provides a foundational atlas of TLS regions in NSCLC and highlights inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1)-high endothelial venules (HEVs) as a potential biomarker, offering insights to guide new immunotherapeutic approaches or enhance the effectiveness of current treatments.    Fig. 1   Study design and cohorts. ( A ) Xenium discovery cohort: profiling of eight resected NSCLC specimens (four neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, four untreated) using spatial single-cell transcriptomics allowed the manual annotation of 90 TLS regions for downstream analyses. ( B ) Biomarker validation cohort: 45 archival NSCLC resections from patients treated with immune-checkpoint blockade after recurrence were interrogated by multiplex immunofluorescence for TLS/HEV markers and linked to overall patient survival                     Materials and methods   Patients and samples  Tissue specimens and clinical records from patients with NSCLC were collected at 14 Japanese institutions between January 2017 and February 2024. Consistent with the KEYNOTE-189, CheckMate-816, and CheckMate-9LA protocols [ 2 ,  4 ,  5 ], patients harboring major EGFR mutations or ALK rearrangements were excluded.  In the xenium discovery cohort, we initially identified 29 patients who underwent surgical resection within the preceding two years, with or without neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy. Patients who achieved clinical complete response after the neoadjuvant therapy or received perioperative radiotherapy were excluded. Furthermore, we selected eight patients showing TLSs enrichment in immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis (as described below) and with an RNA DV200 ≥ 30%. Given the limited tissue from pre-treatment bronchoscopic biopsies, matched pre-/post-treatment pairs were not available, and independent resected specimens were used for Xenium analysis. Therefore, the final analysis included four patients who received neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy and four patients who underwent surgery without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, analyzed as independent patient samples (Supplementary Fig. S2A, B). In the biomarker validation cohort using multiplex-immunofluorescence (MIF), 683 patients who underwent ICB with or without chemotherapy were initially screened. Among these, 575 patients were excluded because the available specimens were derived from bronchoscopy, metastatic-site biopsy, computed tomography-guided needle biopsy, or because no residual tissue remained. Archived lung specimens obtained prior to any immunotherapy exposure were available from 108 surgical cases. Among these, 45 patients who later initiated immunotherapy within two years after postoperative recurrence were enrolled for MIF (as described below), and survival analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3).  Additionally, we retrieved a scRNA-seq dataset comprising 26 breast cancer specimens from the GEO (accession  GSE176078 ) and downloaded an integrated scRNA-seq dataset of 185 NSCLC specimens from Figshare (DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.6222221.v3).    Treatment responses and survival evaluation  Clinical variables, including age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, smoking history, histology, programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score (PD-L1 TPS), clinical stage, and treatment outcomes, were extracted from patient records. PD-L1 TPS was measured with the 22C3 antibody. Radiographic responses were categorized according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1 [ 25 ]. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from chemo-immunotherapy initiation to death or the last follow-up. The data cut-off date was March 31, 2025.    IHC and MIF examination  Chromogenic IHC was performed on 5 μm formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) lung-cancer sections after Tris-EDTA retrieval (pH 9.0, 95 °C, 40 min) and peroxidase quenching (Dako REAL). Serial sections were incubated at 4 °C overnight with primary antibodies including anti-CD3 (Proteintech, #60181-1-Ig, 1:800), anti-CD20 (Proteintech, #60271-1-Ig, 1:1000), and anti-PNAd (BioLegend, clone MECA-79, #120801, 1:100). Detection was performed using an HRP–DAB system following the manufacturers’ instructions. MIF was performed with two four-marker panels. Panel 1: CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), CD23-CL594 (Proteintech, clone 4C7C9, #CL594-60208-2, 1:100), CD3-CL647 (Proteintech, clone 3F3A1, #CL647-60181, 1:100), and CXCL12 (CST, clone D8G6H, #97958, 1:100); Panel 2: MECA-79-AF488 (Invitrogen, clone MECA-79, #53-6-36–82, 1:50), CD31 (Proteintech, clone 3F8E2, #66065-2-Ig, 1:100), CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), and ID1 (CST, clone F2M1J, #23369, 1:100).  Fluorescence was detected using the following secondary antibodies: donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 488, donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 647, donkey anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, 1:500, 1 h, room temperature), and goat anti-rabbit CoraLite Plus 750 (Proteintech, 1:200, 1 h, RT). The slides were mounted in antifade medium with DAPI (Invitrogen) and imaged on an FV3000 confocal microscope (Olympus) with 20×, 40×, and 60× objectives under identical laser and gain settings.    IHC quantification  TLSs were identified with a two-step procedure as previously described [ 26 ]. First, serial sections were immunostained for CD20 (B cells), CD3 (T cells), and PNAd (HEV). TLS-positive specimens showed clusters of T cells surrounding aggregates of B cells. Second, TLSs were divided into three status by B-cell density and follicular architecture: absent, immature, and mature. CXCL12 protein level was quantified using ImageJ (v 2.9.0/1.53t) as the mean percentage of the TLS area with positive staining in three representative fields. Cases above and below the cohort median (excluding TLS-negative samples) were classified as CXCL12-high and CXCL12-low, respectively. ID1 status was determined by counting ID1-positive endothelial cells in HEVs within TLSs across three representative microscopic fields. Specimens with a mean count ≥ 10 and < 10 cells were classified as ID1-high and ID1-low, respectively. Two investigators trained in digital histopathology reviewed the images independently and were blinded to the clinical data. Discrepancies were resolved by joint review, and the final status was verified by an additional pathologist.    Xenium in situ workflow  Five-micron FFPE sections (DV200 ≥ 30%) containing TLSs by IHC were processed using the Xenium FFPE workflow (see 10x Genomics,  CG000601  Rev B). After de-paraffinization, decrosslinking, and Tris-EDTA retrieval, the slides were hybridized overnight at 50 °C with a 430-gene probe set (10 nM each, 380-gene Human Immune-Oncology base panel plus 50 custom endothelial-focused custom genes; Supplementary Table S1), then ligated and amplified by rolling-circle amplification. The prepared slides were run on the Xenium Analyzer, which executed 15 automated cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and stripping, capturing 0.75 μm Z-stacks across the entire 12 × 24 mm imaging area. The on-instrument pipeline stitched fields of view, segmented nuclei/cells from DAPI, and decoded transcripts by maximum-likelihood matching to the gene codebook. Transcripts with calibrated Q-scores ≥ 20 were retained. A cell-by-gene count matrix, segmentation masks; and morphology images were exported for downstream analysis.    Xenium in situ analyses  Cell segmentation morphology images generated by the Xenium Analyzer were co-registered with the corresponding H&E images, after which every TLS was manually delineated, and the constituent cells were extracted for downstream analysis (Supplementary Fig. S4). TLS boundaries were drawn to encompass contiguous clusters of immune cells. All spatial transcriptomic analyses in this study were restricted to cells located within these manually annotated TLS regions of interest. Tumor parenchyma outside the TLS boundaries was not included in the expression matrices used for any downstream analyses.  All analyses were carried out using R software (v 4.4.2) and Python (v 3.12.9). Using Seurat package (v 5.2.1), we generated a separate Seurat object for each TLS and removed low-quality cells (< 5 detected genes and < 10 total transcript counts). All TLS objects were then pooled into a single Seurat object for downstream processing. Gene expression matrices were normalized using the NormalizeData function, variable features were identified with the FindVariableFeatures function, and linear scaling was applied using the ScaleData function. PCA was performed with the RunPCA function and the optimal number of principal components (PCs) was selected from the ElbowPlot. Batch effects arising from sample identity were corrected by applying the RunHarmony function to the PCA embeddings, and clustering was conducted on the Harmony-integrated PCs using the Louvain algorithm [ 27 ]. The same embeddings were used to generate Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualizations.  Because spatial transcriptomics can misassign transcripts to neighboring cells, the cell-type annotation did not rely solely on canonical markers. Rather, candidate markers for each cluster were identified using FindMarkers function (log fold-change > 0.20;  P  < 0.01), and the resulting labels were imported into Xenium Explorer, where they were cross-validated against cellular morphology and histological context (e.g., endothelial cells continuity). Higher-resolution analyses were performed for endothelial cells, with each population re-extracted into a new Seurat object, dimensional reduction and clustering repeated as described above, and cell-type identities refined (Supplementary Table S2) [ 15 ,  28 – 31 ]. Mixed clusters were similarly reclassified, and the final cell-type labels were appended to the metadata of the main object.  Differentially expressed genes were identified for each cell type with two-sided t-tests, with significance thresholds of |log₂ fold change| ≥ 0.20 and  P  < 0.01. Genes that met these criteria were subjected to Gene Ontology overrepresentation analysis to elucidate the biological pathways that were preferentially affected in each comparison. Cell–cell communications (CCIs) were reconstructed using CellChat package (v 2.1.2), which quantitatively infers ligand–receptor interaction networks from scRNA-seq profiles. To place these interactions in their spatial context, we subsequently analyzed the CCIs within each field of view, including TLSs, using stLearn (v 0.4.10).    Statistical analyses  Continuous variables and dichotomous variables are summarized as medians with inter-quartile ranges and absolute counts with percentages, respectively. Group differences in categorical data were assessed with Pearson’s χ² or Fisher’s exact tests, as appropriate. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare TLS counts and the cellular compositions stratified by TLS maturity and treatment arm. OS was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier curves (log-rank test) and modelled using Cox proportional-hazards regression. The independent correlates of TLS maturation and CXCL12/ID1 status were identified with multivariable logistic regression. All analyses were performed in R (v 4.4.2), and two-sided P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.     Results   Spatial single-cell atlas reveals B-cell-dominated TLS architecture independent of neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy  The eight-patient Xenium discovery cohort is summarized in Table  1 . Apart from a slightly younger median age in the ICB plus chemotherapy arm, the two groups were well balanced for sex, clinical stage, histological subtype and PD-L1 TPS. Neoadjuvant treatment produced one pathological complete response, with partial responses in the remaining cases. A density map from Xenium Explorer demonstrated that a composite oncogenic signature, based on  CEACAM6 ,  EGFR ,  EPCAM ,  ERBB2 ,  ERBB3 ,  MET ,  MUC5AC  and  TMPRSS2 , closely tracked with therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, serial sections confirmed PNAd-positive HEV in all TLSs (Supplementary Fig. S5). After filtering, 319,909 cells were retained and classified based on canonical markers into 16 cell-type clusters: conventional B cells (Bconv), follicular B cells (FoB), proliferating B cells, conventional CD4⁺ T cells (CD4_Tconv), follicular-helper T cells (Tfh), regulatory T cells (Treg), CD8⁺ T cells, plasma cells, macrophages, mature and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (mDC, pDC), mast cells, neutrophils, endothelial cells, fibroblasts and tumor cells (Fig.  2 A). Unintegrated UMAPs showed specimen-specific clustering; however, harmony correction merged cells from all eight samples into shared lineage islands, indicating effective removal of batch effects (Fig.  2 B). TLS maturation reshapes immune niches and improves survival under cancer immunotherapy  To minimize therapy-related bias, TLS maturation was interrogated exclusively in untreated controls. Representative Xenium Explorer and MIF findings readily distinguished compact, mantle-ringed B-cell follicles from loosely organized, T-cell–rich aggregates, designating the former as mature and the latter as immature.  CXCL13 ,  CXCR5 ,  FCER2  and  MS4A1  were highly concentrated in mature cores; their combined expression was converted into a “mature-TLS score” with AddModuleScore function (Fig.  3 A) [ 34 ,  35 ]. Using a threshold of 0 separated 22 mature (≥ 0) and 26 immature (< 0) structures (Fig.  3 B), and visual overlays of TLS maturation showed near-perfect concordance with histology (Fig.  3 C). Area-normalized transcriptional profiling of the 13 chemokines and their receptors revealed a sharp dichotomy (Fig.  3 D): mature TLSs contained significantly more  CXCL13  and  CXCR4 , whereas immature TLSs were enriched for  CCL2 ,  CCL3 ,  CCL4 ,  CCL5 ,  CCL8 ,  CCL18  and the IFN-inducible  CXCL9–11  cluster. TLS-area–adjusted cell counts mirrored these findings, with higher densities of every B-cell subset in mature TLSs, and predominantly CD8⁺ T cells, macrophages, mDCs and endothelial cells in their immature counterparts (Fig.  3 E). In mature TLSs, fibroblasts showed higher  CXCL12 , whereas FoBs exhibited elevated  CXCR4  [ 36 ]. Tfh cells expressed abundant  CXCL13  together with  CXCR5  on B cells [ 33 ]. In contrast, immature TLSs exhibited a Th1-skewed inflammatory milieu characterized by  CXCL9  from IFN-γ-responsive macrophages and DCs, and higher  IFIT3  in CD8⁺ T cells. Endothelial transcriptomics reinforced this functional divergence: mature TLS vasculature preferentially expressed PNAd-associated genes, such as  CHST4  and  B3GNT3  together with adhesion molecules, including  SELP  and  ICAM1 , whereas immature TLSs overexpressed the HEV-developmental receptors  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14  (Fig.  3 F and Supplementary Fig. S6). Gene Ontology analysis echoed these contrasts, identifying enrichment of adaptive B-cell programs in mature TLSs and pathways governing lymphocyte migration, cell–cell adhesion, and activation thresholds in immature TLSs (Fig.  3 G).  Kaplan–Meier curves in immunotherapy-treated patients demonstrated that mature TLSs conferred a substantial survival advantage over immature or absent TLSs (median OS 60.2 vs. 21.4 months; log-rank  P  = 0.037) (Fig.  3 H). Collectively, these spatial and transcriptional features characterize TLS maturation states and demonstrate their prognostic relevance in patients receiving immunotherapy.    ID1-high HEVs in mature TLS are associated with better survival in patients receiving immunotherapy  Unsupervised UMAP analysis of the pre-processed, normalized endothelial subset resolved two transcriptionally discrete vascular clusters: high endothelial cell (HEC) and blood endothelial cell (BEC) (Fig.  4 A and Supplementary Fig. S7). The HEC cluster was characterized by robust expression of classical HEV genes, including  ACKR1 ,  SELP ,  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14 , confirming its HEV-like phenotype (Fig.  4 B) [ 30 ]. MIF of resected samples corroborated the spatial coexistence of both HEC- and BEC-type vessels within mature TLSs in situ (Fig.  4 C). Differential-expression analysis of HECs revealed significant upregulation of  ID1  in mature TLSs compared with immature TLSs (Fig.  4 D,  P  < 0.05). Compared with the other ID family members,  ID2  and  ID4 ,  ID1  was selectively expressed in endothelial cells, with the highest levels observed in HECs (Fig.  4 E, F). We further re-analyzed an integrated scRNA-seq dataset comprising 185 NSCLC samples to validate ID-family expression in the vascular compartment [ 19 ].  ID1  expression was largely confined to malignant epithelial and endothelial cells. Within the endothelial lineage, its expression was observed across several subpopulations, including mature HECs. In mature HECs,  ID1  was frequently expressed, whereas  ID2  and  ID4  were rarely detected (Supplementary Fig. S8). These findings are broadly consistent with our spatial transcriptomic analysis.    Fig. 4   Endothelial-focused spatial transcriptomic and MIF analyses within TLSs. In the biomarker validation cohort ( n  = 45), 18 patients (40%) had ID1-high HEVs, whereas the remaining 27 patients (60%) had ID1-low HEVs or lacked mature TLSs (baseline characteristics are summarized in Supplementary Table S3). Patients with tumors with ID1-high HEVs showed a markedly higher objective response rate (61%) compared with those with ID1-low HEVs (17%) or without mature TLSs (7%) (Fig.  4 L,  P  < 0.05). Likewise, Kaplan–Meier analysis showed a pronounced survival advantage among patients with ID1-high HEVs, with median OS not reached versus 21.4 months in the ID1-low HEVs/absent mature TLSs groups (Fig.  4 M, log-rank  P  < 0.001). Finally, responders and non-responders showed no clear differences in baseline characteristics within the ID1-high group, suggesting the limits of ID1-high HEVs as a predictor (Supplementary Table S4). Together, these data identify ID1-high HEVs as a functional hallmark of mature TLSs and a robust biomarker of enhanced immunotherapy efficacy and survival in NSCLC. UMAP embedding and stacked bar plot reveal that, although the two cohorts harbored a comparable number of TLS (Wilcoxon  p  = 0.88), ICB therapy was associated with a trend toward a more B-cell-dominant intralesional profile (Wilcoxon  p  = 0.11), whereas control TLSs contained B- and T-cell compartments in roughly equal proportions (Fig.  5 A, B). Area-normalized chemokine profiling revealed a treatment-specific dichotomy: control TLSs expressed higher levels of inflammatory  CCL4 ,  CCL18 ,  CCL21  and  CXCL9-11  cluster, whereas ICB-treated TLSs showed selective upregulation of  CXCL12  together with its receptor  CXCR4 .  CXCL13  expression per TLS area remained comparable between groups despite increased  CXCR5  expression in ICB-treated TLSs (Fig.  5 C). TLS-area–normalized cell counts confirmed treatment-specific re-patterning, with increased conventional and follicular B cell densities under ICB therapy, whereas central-proliferating B cells were unchanged and exhibited lower  MKI67  expression. While the number of Tfh cells increased, their  CXCL13  output decreased sharply. Although fibroblast numbers were comparable,  CXCL12  expression increased markedly in the ICB cohort.  CXCR4  levels also increased consistently across these cell types (Fig.  5 D, E). Furthermore, spatial CCI maps demonstrated that TLSs in ICB–treated tumors displayed stronger  CXCL12–CXCR4  signaling than those in untreated controls (Fig.  5 F). Within this pathway, fibroblasts showed the strongest communication probabilities with follicular B cells (Fig.  5 G). Nearest-neighbor distances between fibroblasts and FoBs were comparable in the control and ICB cohort (Fig.  5 H). Among the fibroblast subsets, PDGFRA⁺ fibroblasts were identified as the population most likely to interact with FoBs through the CXCL12–CXCR4 axis (Supplementary Fig. S9) [ 37 ]. High  CXCL12  expression within TLSs has been proposed to correlate with greater immune-cell infiltration and favor antitumor activity [ 38 ]. Consistent with this notion, patients with NSCLC treated with immunotherapy for tumors harboring CXCL12-high TLSs showed a significantly longer OS compared with those with CXCL12-low or TLS-negative tumors (median OS 60.2 vs. 26.6 months; log-rank  P  = 0.014) (Fig.  5 I, J). In summary, immunotherapy-driven tumor regression enhanced  CXCL12–CXCR4  signaling, suggesting that patients with TLSs bearing this  CXCL12 -high niche may have a greater survival benefit from ICB therapy. ICB–treated tumors contained fewer PNAd-positive HEV per square millimeter than control, indicating a treatment-related reduction in HEV density (Fig.  6 A, B). TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors exhibited a transcriptional shift in which adhesion genes including  SELE  and  SELP  together with the PNAd-biosynthetic module — B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1  and  ST3GAL4 — were likewise suppressed, and the differentiation brake  ID1  fell sharply, along with  ID2  (Fig.  6 C, D). In contrast, angio-remodeling transcripts, including  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  VEGFA ,  APLN ,  APLNR , and  FLT1 , increased. However, VEGFA expression within endothelial cells was minimal, and the ligand was predominantly supplied by fibroblasts rather than by HEVs themselves (Supplementary Fig. 10). Gene Ontology analysis consistently shows that ICB therapy redirected HECs from an immune-recruitment program toward vascular remodeling: genes that are upregulated in the treated group clustered within angiogenesis pathways, whereas those enriched in controls were related to immune trafficking (Fig.  6 E). Furthermore, ICB therapy significantly decreased an adhesion signature per TLS, defined by  B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1 ,  ST3GAL4 ,  SELE ,  SELP ,  ICAM1  and  VCAM1 , while simultaneously amplifying an angio-remodel signature comprising  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  APLN ,  APLNR ,  FLT1  and  TEK  (Fig.  6 F, G). Functionally, the normalized counts of conventional B, CD4⁺ T, and CD8⁺ T cells located within 100 μm of a HEC were significantly reduced in the ICB cohort (Fig.  6 H,  P  < 0.05). Finally, MIF showed markedly reduced ID1 protein in TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors compared with controls, mirroring the transcriptomic downregulation described above (Fig.  6 I, J). In summary, TLS-associated HEVs potentially shift phenotypically with TLS maturation and treatment. In immature TLS, HEVs first express the LTβR axis and homing chemokines, recruiting lymphocytes via nascent HEC cuffs with BECs. During maturation,  ID1  increases, and classical adhesion features together with the PNAd-synthetic enzyme set predominates, yielding a fully functional “mature HEV.” ICB ultimately regresses tumors and drives the vessels into a remodeled endothelial state: ID1 levels fall sharply, the adhesion/PNAd module contracts, and lymphocyte influx diminishes, while vascular-remodeling genes are induced, preserving structural plasticity (Fig.  6 K). In the present study, we aimed to map how TLS composition and endothelial dynamics varied with maturation and treatment, and link these mechanistic insights to clinical outcomes to elucidate their contribution to TLS-mediated antitumor immunity.  This study provides an integrated spatial-omics framework unifying the cellular and clinical dimensions of TLSs in NSCLC, particularly in endothelial populations. By combining high-sensitivity in situ transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence, and immunotherapy-related clinical outcomes, we delineate three key principles: (i) TLS maturation establishes novel immune niches in NSCLC, (ii) ID1-high HEVs within mature TLSs confer clinical benefit, and (iii) ICB therapy reprograms HEVs from a lymphocyte-recruiting phenotype to a vascular-reprogramming state while enhancing a  CXCL12-CXCR4  niche.  Spatial transcriptomics is indispensable for analyzing TLS biology. TLSs juxtapose lymphoid, myeloid, and stromal elements in complex three-dimensional assemblies. Therefore, only methods that preserve tissue coordinates and resolve individual cells can reveal their true organization. The Xenium In Situ platforms provide sub-micrometer, in-situ detection of transcripts, enabling the visual validation of cell annotations and tracking of follicles, vessels, and related microstructure continuity throughout an entire TLS. By applying this platform, we profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells at single-cell resolution to obtain a nearly exhaustive annotation of every anatomical component. We further expanded the standard immuno-oncology panel with vascular-specific genes, allowing cytokine and chemokine quantification across all cell types, with a focus on endothelial cells.  Consistent with our observations, studies in both hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer show that mature TLSs are characterized by  CXCL13 -rich, B-cell-dominated cores, whereas immature aggregates show enrichment of  CXCL9-11  and Th1-skewed signatures [ 23 ,  39 ]. While single-cell studies on HEVs in human tumors are limited, analogous analyses in human lymph nodes are increasing [ 30 ,  40 ]. These nodal datasets have demonstrated that PNAd-positive HEVs form a discrete endothelial cluster characterized by high expression of adhesion genes such as  SELE ,  SELP ,  B3GNT3  and  CHST4 , whereas BECs segregate as a separate population lacking immune-trafficking functions. These observations are consistent with our findings, supporting the conclusion that TLS maturation is conserved across different organs and tumor types.  ID1 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcriptional regulator lacking a DNA-binding motif. Instead, it heterodimerizes with canonical bHLH factors, blocking lineage-specific transcription and sustaining a proliferative, undifferentiated state. Its expression is induced by a variety of upstream cues, including BMP/SMAD1-5, TGF-β, VEGF-A/VEGFR2, hypoxia-stabilized HIF-1α, Wnt/β-catenin, and inflammatory cytokines [ 41 ]. In tumors,  ID1  is enriched mainly in malignant and endothelial cells and promotes metastasis and angiogenesis; therefore, its overexpression correlates with poor prognosis. However, its involvement in HEVs remains unreported [ 42 ]. Lyden et al. showed that physiological  ID  expression is indispensable for angiogenesis in  ID  knockout mouse models, in which endothelial cells lacking  ID1  emerged in tumor xenografts but did not lumenize or generate properly branched vessels [ 43 ]. Accordingly, ID family genes are critical for synchronizing endothelial differentiation with the invasive expansion of the vascular network. Typically, high  ID1  expression in bulk lung tumor tissue is linked to poor prognosis, whereas our data show that within TLSs, elevated  ID1  levels trend toward improved clinical outcomes [ 44 ]. Such  ID1 -like “context-dependent inversions” are likewise observed for several other genes within the TLS compartment. Although the  CXCL12–CXCR4  axis is classically pro-tumorigenic outside TLSs, promoting metastasis, angiogenesis, and immune evasion through ERK1/2, Ras, p38 MAPK, PLC/MAPK, and JNK cascades [ 45 ], CXCL12 expression in combined hepatocellular–cholangiocarcinoma correlates positively with TLS density, TLS maturation, and favorable prognosis, suggesting that within TLSs this axis may instead support lymphoid organization and maturation [ 38 ]. In parallel, a recent study in hepatocellular carcinoma demonstrated that chemotherapy-induced TLS formation is likewise driven by CXCL12–CXCR4–mediated recruitment of immune and stromal cells, further reinforcing the notion that this axis can acquire a TLS-promoting role in specific therapeutic contexts [ 46 ]. Collectively, these observations highlight that signaling pathways traditionally viewed as oncogenic can adopt distinct, TLS-restricted functions, underscoring the need to dissect TLS-specific vascular pathways when developing HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.  CXCL13 is a recognized marker of follicular TLS cores and favorable outcome [ 14 ,  47 ]. In our data, the CXCL13 load per TLS was comparable between the control and ICB-treated cohorts, whereas CXCR5 expression was increased in ICB-treated TLSs. This dissociation suggests that ICB does not globally amplify CXCL13 production itself, but rather selectively enhances the responsiveness of B cells and Tfh to a relatively stable CXCL13 field. By contrast, knowledge regarding chemokines other than CXCL13 remains limited. Our data show that ICB selectively augments  CXCL12  expression in fibroblasts. Although the mechanistic link between PD-1 signaling and  CXCL12  induction remains to be elucidated, the increase in CXCL12 parallels a modest association between PD-L1 TPS and TLS maturation [ 13 ]. Consistent with independent spatial omics studies, mature TLSs displayed strikingly high  CXCL12  levels, mirroring the  CXCL13  pattern, suggesting that, in this compartmentalized niche,  CXCL12  may emerge as a biomarker of durable benefits in immunotherapy-treated patients rather than a canonical pro-tumorigenic signal [ 38 ]. Nevertheless, multivariate models incorporating TLS maturation as a confounder did not identify CXCL12 as an independent predictor, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation. In contrast, ID1 retained its independent prognostic significance even after adjustment, despite possible unmeasured immunosuppressive factors limiting its predictive value. Although our study is retrospective and does not allow longitudinal tracking of individual HEVs, one possible interpretation is that an ID1-high, functionally active HEV niche is well established at baseline in tumors that ultimately respond to ICB. In contrast, such an ID1-high niche may be insufficiently formed or inadequately maintained in non-responders. These post-treatment changes do not contradict the prognostic relevance of baseline ID1-high HEVs. Baseline ID1-high HEVs in untreated tumors reflect a reactive, lymphocyte-recruiting program that facilitates antitumor immunity and predicts ICI benefit, similar to reports showing that pre-existing HEV-rich tumors are associated with improved clinical outcomes [ 48 ]. In contrast, the ID1-low, PNAd-low, angiogenic-signature–high state observed after ICI likely represents a physiological reprogramming process during the resolution of inflammation, in which HEVs transition from a recruitment-competent phenotype to a vascular-maintenance or retention-type state. Thus, the baseline predictive role of ID1 and its post-therapy reduction correspond to distinct temporal phases of HEV biology rather than opposing biological effects. In summary, our work illustrates ID1 as a novel predictive and monitoring biomarker, although its regulatory mechanisms require further research.  The principal strength of this study was the application of Xenium In Situ, which preserved the native continuity of TLSs and their vasculature while providing single-cell resolution. Conventional scRNA-seq–derived “TLS-mimic” datasets cannot attain this fidelity: our approach profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells and retained intact follicles and vessels, which allowed the direct assessment of CCIs and HEV-mediated lymphocyte recruitment. We then validated the markers identified through this spatial screening in independent immunotherapy cohorts, thereby establishing ID1 as a clinically relevant biomarker associated with survival. However, the study has several limitations. First, the target-gene panel was relatively small. Although the default set captures core cell-type markers, it does not include essential TLS genes such as  BCL6  and  AICDA , which should be custom-added for deeper analyses. Second, the discovery and validation cohorts were modest in size and retrospective in design; thus, selection bias was possible, and the generalizability of the findings is limited. To address these issues, a prospective study with a larger patient cohort is warranted.  In conclusion, our data revealed a link between TLS maturation or ICB therapy and HEC differentiation, in which  ID1  plays a pivotal regulatory role. In mature TLSs, HECs display high  ID1  expression, actively recruit lymphocytes, and are associated with favorable clinical outcomes. However, after ICB induced tumor regressions,  ID1  and adhesion transcripts in HECs decreased sharply, lymphocyte ingress wanes, and a vascular remodeling-signature was induced. Therefore, ID1 has emerged as a dynamic biomarker in patients treated with immunotherapy. Collectively, these findings provide a mechanistic framework and a practical biomarker set for HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.    Supplementary Information

evidence_text: Iron-catalyzed oxidative stress reveals an exposome-related ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche in BRCA1-linked renal carcinogenesis. Early cancer initiation under chronic oxidative stress requires the survival of epithelial cells that should otherwise be eliminated by regulated cell death. However, the spatial and morphological identity of such stress-adapted cells remains poorly defined. Here, we integrated Xenium single-cell spatial transcriptomics, quantitative nuclear morphometrics, mitochondrial analyses, and human cancer datasets to investigate iron-driven renal carcinogenesis in Brca1(L63X/+) rats. Ferric nitrilotriacetate exposure induced dynamic remodeling of proximal tubular epithelium, characterized by loss of homeostatic transport and mitochondrial programs, and activation of Myc, Met, Lcn2, Anxa2 and iron-handling genes. BRCA1 haploinsufficiency expanded a karyomegalic proximal tubular state associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, chromatin hyperchromasia, nuclear remodeling, and ferroptosis-resistant transcriptional features. Subclassification of karyomegalic cells identified distinct stress-adaptive populations, including a BRCA1-associated K2 state enriched for Myc/Met/Lcn2 signaling and preferentially embedded within a pro-oncogenic epithelial-stromal microenvironment. Of note, neighboring non-karyomegalic proximal tubular cells acquired related iron-handling and survival-biased programs, indicating that karyomegaly marks a broader pre-neoplastic field rather than an isolated abnormality. Human TCGA renal cancer analyses and morphometric assessment of BRCA1-mutant breast tissue further supported the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated gene modules and nuclear remodeling. These findings define a spatially organized, ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche as an early lesion in iron-driven carcinogenesis and establish quantitative nuclear morphology as a functional readout of exposome-related oxidative stress adaptation in genetically susceptible tissues.
