As identified by gene set enrichment analysis, gene expression relating to oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in ICI-AIN samples, and tubular epithelial cells rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation because of their high energy demand. 28 Using the spatial niche data, we found this reduction localized mostly to the niches related to parts of the kidney tubule ( Figure 4 c). The gene module score for oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in the injured as compared with the noninjured proximal tubule niches. However, in both injured and healthy proximal tubule niches in AIN samples, there was an additive reduction in oxidative phosphorylation gene signatures in multivariable linear regression models ( Supplementary Figure S8 ). IFN-γ-signaling within the noninjured proximal tubule niches was strongly anticorrelated with a gene signature for oxidative phosphorylation ( Figure 4 d). Another hallmark effect of IFN-γ is the polarization of myeloid cells into a proinflammatory, tissue-aggressive state, as we observed in the “inflammatory myeloid” cluster ( Figure 3 a–b). 29 Within this cluster, we found the expression of genes typical for a proinflammatory myeloid polarization (such as MMP9 , IDO1 ), as well as the highest gene expression signature of an IFN-γ response ( Figure 4 e–f). In summary, CD8 + T cell-derived IFN-γ was associated with reduced oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells and a proinflammatory signature in inflammatory myeloid cells. Tissue-Resident Macrophage Niches Associate With Fibrosis Finally, we investigated which immune cell niches were associated with fibrosis in ICI-AIN. To this end, we calculated the probability of neighboring an area of fibrosis for each subtype of immune niche, normalized for the relative abundance of immune niches. The CD8+ infiltrated and tissue-resident myeloid cell niches in ICI-AIN were most likely to neighbor fibrotic niches compared with the ICI-ATN group ( Figure 4 g). Additionally, we defined a fibrotic niche transcriptional signature as the top 100 differentially expressed genes for the fibrosis niches and calculated a signature score for each immune subniche. Consistent with the neighborhood analysis, the tissue-resident myeloid niches had the highest fibrosis signature score ( Figure 4 h), highlighting their role in a fibrotic tissue response. Discussion Here, we have described the landscape of immune infiltration and fibrosis in the kidneys of patients with ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN. Using high-resolution spatial transcriptomic analysis, we elucidated key features of ICI-AIN, including a strong activation of IFN-γ/STAT1 signaling, a reduction in oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells, and a heterogeneous immune cell infiltration. Based on the Tessera algorithm 19 for the identification of niches with similar transcriptional profiles, we were able to identify biologically meaningful, functional units, thereby circumventing the problems associated with cell segmentation. Some niches corresponded to histoanatomical parts of the kidney, like the glomeruli or specific segments of the tubule, allowing us to compare the gene expression within specific kidney regions. Other niche types corresponded to pathological changes, including immune cell infiltration and fibrosis. Clustering-based analyses enabled us to investigate the heterogeneity of the immune cell infiltrate in detail, highlighting how TLS-like structures, myeloid cell-dominant inflammation, and fibrotic processes happen in parallel within the ICI-AIN-damaged kidney. Analyzing the spatial expression of chemokine and/or receptor pairs enabled us to understand the mechanisms that determine the architecture of these meta-structures. Our analyses found that CD8 + T cells are associated with the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN given the limited control of ICI-ATN ( Figure 5 ). T cell infiltration appeared to play a functional role in all the immune cell niches we identified, and T cell-related genes were among the most abundant in all niches. These T cells, expressing markers of repeated activation like PD1, CTLA4, and LAG3, seemed to coordinate the recruitment and activation of other immune cells by the expression of CXCL13 (attracting B and T cells and forming TLS-like structures) and IFN-γ (inducing an inflammatory myeloid phenotype). These inflammatory myeloid cells, in turn, may have induced tissue damage by producing metalloproteases like MMP9 and by recruiting additional CXCR3-expressing inflammatory cells producing CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11. Figure 5 Schematic of the inferred pathophysiology in ICI-AIN with a focus on the role of CD8 + T cells. CD8 + T cells with transcriptional markers of tissue-residency and repeated stimulation are the main producers of IFN-γ. IFN-γ reduces oxidative phosphorylation in kidney tubules and induces a proinflammatory program in myeloid cells. These proinflammatory myeloid cells lead to tissue damage and also produce the chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11, attracting additional CXCR3 + lymphocytes, including additional CD8 + T cells. CD8 + T cells also produce CXCL13, a chemokine that attracts B cells and induces the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures in the kidney. Notably, CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN recapitulated features associated with T cells of the tumor microenvironment with transcriptional features of exhaustion and instigation of TLS structures by the production of CXCL13. 30 , 31 , 32 Plasma cells also showed increased abundance in the ICI-AIN samples, and we hypothesize that these indicate productive B-T cell interactions in these TLS-like structures. Plasma cells have also been identified in ICI-associated myocarditis; however, no antibodies against myocardial antigens were identified. 12 Although T cells in ICI-ATN samples showed a transcriptional signature typical of short-lived effector cells (expressing KLRG1 and CX3CR1 ), the CD8 + T cells in ICI-AIN expressed more HOBIT ( ZNF683 ), CD103 ( ITGAE ), and CXCR6, markers of tissue-resident memory cells. 33 Interestingly, a CD8 + T cell subset with high expression of HOBIT was identified in the peripheral blood of a patient with kidney allograft rejection after ICI treatment. 34 A similar signature of ITGAE + tissue-resident T cells was recently reported in ICI-related colitis. 11 It is therefore plausible that CD8 + tissue-resident memory T cells, disinhibited by ICI treatment, are the primary cell type that initiates the inflammatory cascade observed in ICI-AIN. Our analyses also implicated niches with a high density of a tissue-resident transcription profile in the development of kidney fibrosis. This is consistent with recent reports highlighting the role of a similar population in fibrotic damage in lupus nephritis. 35 , 36 Although we reported the spatial association of these niches with fibrotic area, future research is needed to determine if these cells mediate fibrosis or protect against further damage. The immunological changes we observed may inform the selection of novel treatment targets in ICI-AIN. Currently, ICI-AIN is treated by holding or discontinuing ICIs and administering glucocorticoids, which may compromise anti-tumor immune response. 37 , 38 Drugs targeting IFN-γ and its receptors, and especially drugs such as baricitinib and ruxolitinib—which target the downstream signaling of Janus Kinase and/or STAT—may thus have greater utility in treating ICI-AIN. To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive spatial data of ICI-AKI to date; however, there were limitations. Alignment of kidney structures with spatial transcriptomic areas was poor, and high-resolution images of H&E stainings were performed on serial sections. Furthermore, kidney biopsies from patients with ICI-AIN show great heterogeneity, and the small number of samples analyzed, along with the lack of inclusion of “healthy” controls, may have limited our ability to explore key differences. Notably, medullary cell types and niches were overrepresented in the ICI-AIN samples because of higher representation of kidney medulla in ICI-AIN samples. However, we chose the ICI-ATN group as controls as they share important confounding features with the ICI-AIN group (malignant disease, cancer treatment, and unspecific kidney tissue changes caused by AKI). Additionally, the commercial Xenium 5K panel may have limited utility in providing insight into cell types within the nephron. Methods for cellular segmentation in spatial transcriptomic and proteomic analyses are still an area of active investigation; thus, transcripts of neighboring cells may spill over and dilute marker gene identification, especially in areas with challenging cell morphologies, such as the glomerulus. Current spatial transcriptomic approaches result in relatively sparse data, which can lead to biases. For example, the emphasis on CD8 + T cells in our data could, at least in part, be explained by the higher transcript density of CD8A compared with CD4 . Although we used a niche-based approach to mitigate these limitations, orthogonal approaches like single-cell transcriptomics in ICI-AIN will be needed to phenotype infiltrating immune cells at higher resolution. In summary, we used spatial transcriptomics to show that IFN-γ-producing CD8 + T cells may be implicated in the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN, and that CD8 + T cell-derived IFN-γ likely induces a proinflammatory state in myeloid cells, with increased tissue production of CXCL9, 10, and 11. Future studies with a larger number of samples will be needed to validate our findings and investigate the association of specific immune niche subsets with disease severity and/or refractoriness, treatment response, and likelihood of kidney recovery. evidence_text:
Unraveling lncRNA diversity at a single cell resolution and in a spatial context across different cancer types. Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) participate in gene regulation underlying development and disease. Overcoming inherent limitations of bulk sequencing lncRNA analysis, we leveraged single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data to analyze 219,442 potential lncRNAs identified by the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline across 13 cancer types. The lncRNA functions were assessed by identifying their cell-type specificity and spatial distributions across different tissue regions. Comparing with five existing databases, we confirmed shared lncRNAs and found 94,795 unannotated lncRNAs. The identified lncRNAs were experimentally validated across seven cancer types using three single-cell-resolution ST platforms and two long-read ST sequencing methods, encompassing both targeted and untargeted approaches. Genome-wide colocalization of lncRNAs with regulatory features, disease variants and pairwise spatial autocorrelation with protein-coding genes suggest potential functional roles. We built a free, fast and user-friendly database 'SPanC-Lnc' on AWS cloud. SPanC-Lnc will enable discovery of potentially functional lncRNAs specific for cell populations within heterogeneous tissues, providing new biological insights. Main  Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) constitute the majority of the permissively transcribed genome. Despite this, the majority of our knowledge about transcriptional events is limited to the 1–2% of the genome that encodes proteins  1  . With advancements in high-throughput technologies, it has become increasingly apparent that lncRNAs are of functional relevance, contributing to diseases like cancer where they are often misregulated  2  .  The lncRNAs serve as a valuable class of molecular targets for disease identification; however, their detection has been constrained by factors such as their low abundance, cell-type-specific expression patterns and the reliance of existing computational tools on previous annotations  3  . Previous studies on lncRNAs have predominantly relied on bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data, which unfortunately results in the loss of cell-type information and tissue spatial context, both of which are essential for understanding transcriptional regulation in developmental and diseased states. The spatial information provides valuable insights into a transcript’s location within a tissue, its neighboring cells, colocalizing transcripts or proteins and their interacting partners, thereby enhancing our comprehension of biological processes.  Advanced technologies such as single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) sequence transcripts at the single-cell level while preserving spatial information. Up to 40% of lncRNAs are polyadenylated and an additional 40% of them are bimorphic  4  . Thus, using a polyA-capture protocol, such as 10x Visium, these transcripts can be analyzed. Recent studies using scRNA-seq for breast cancer samples  5 , 6   evaluated known (annotated) lncRNAs at a single-cell level. Other studies claiming to have analyzed the ‘spatial transcriptome’ of lncRNAs have typically examined lncRNA expression across different bulk tissues, rather than capturing the nuanced expression patterns of lncRNAs within a tissue section  7 , 8  . These studies did not explore novel unannotated lncRNAs. Several methods for novel transcript identification have been established for bulk sequencing data  9 , 10  . Applying these methods to ST and scRNA-seq data would not only facilitate the expansion of annotations but also unveil additional layers of information regarding lncRNAs, including cell-type specificity and spatial context to reveal physical manifestation of their crosstalk with protein-coding genes. Although these technologies have not yet addressed the identification of non-polyadenylated lncRNAs or the entire spectrum of rare lncRNAs, creating a repository of potential lncRNAs detected through cutting-edge ST technologies would establish a robust foundation for biological discovery.  In this study, we combined large datasets from the spatially resolved RNA sequencing by 10x Visium and single-cell resolution scRNA-seq by 10x Chromium to discover lncRNAs in tissues from 13 different cancer types, along with cross-validation on samples from the more recent technologies like STOmics, Takara Bio Seeker and Xenium in situ. We demonstrated new types of analyses to identify potential functions of lncRNAs. While previous pan-cancer studies have examined clinically relevant lncRNAs  11 – 13  , this study constitutes a large-scale, spatially resolved investigation of uncharacterized or new potential lncRNAs, integrating cell-type-specific information to advance our understanding of their roles in cancer (Supplementary Table  1 ). The annotations and lncRNA expression data of each tissue are accessible through the interactive website ‘SPanC-Lnc’: Spatial and Single Cell Pan-Cancer Atlas of lncRNAs at  https://spanclnc.click/ . Researchers and clinicians can leverage this resource to gain deeper insights into the roles of lncRNAs in cancer biology.    Results   Identification of potential lncRNAs in spatial and single-cell datasets  Samples from 28 previously published in-house ST and 24 scRNA-seq samples across 13 cancer types were analyzed for potential novel lncRNAs (Fig.  1a ) using the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline  10  . The cumulative expression of all unannotated transcriptionally active regions (uTARs) detected in each sample was projected on the corresponding tissues and compared to that of the cumulative coding gene expression. Three representative examples for different cancer types are displayed in Fig.  1b . uTAR and coding gene expression for the remaining samples are also shown in Supplementary Figs.  1  and  2 , respectively. The expression of several previously identified cancer-specific lncRNAs was also visualized (Supplementary Fig.  3 ). It is worth noting that while lncRNAs like  MALAT1  and  NORAD  were abundantly expressed across the tissue sections in various samples (Supplementary Fig.  3a ), others displayed a certain degree of tissue specificity. For instance, both  PICSAR  and  LINC00520 , known to be squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)-specific  14  , were markedly more expressed in cutaneous SCC and head and neck (H&N) oropharyngeal SCC (OPSCC) compared to the other cancer types. In contrast, while  PICSAR  and  LINC00520  were either absent or expressed at lower levels in breast and colorectal cancer (CRC),  TINCR  (known to play oncogenic roles in breast cancer  15 , 16  ) was highly expressed in breast cancer samples (Supplementary Fig.  3b ).  TINCR  is also known to be oncogenic in OPSCC and tumor suppressing in SCC and highly expressed in our representative samples. Similarly,  KCNQ1OT1  (commonly implicated in CRC prognosis  17 , 18  ) showed higher expression in the CRC sample compared to other lncRNAs expressed in this sample.  Fig. 1   Pan-cancer identification of novel lncRNAs from spatial and single-cell data.   a , Different cancer types used from public scRNA-seq and previously published in-house ST datasets for lncRNA detection, further confirmed on high resolution spatial technologies. uTARs as of GENOCDE v.43 were first identified using the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline on a per-sample basis; overlapping uTARs across samples were merged to derive a nonredundant set of cuTARs, which form the final lncRNA annotations in our database. Numbers highlighted in red indicate the number of cuTARs detected for each cancer type, followed by the number of samples analyzed within square brackets.  b , uTAR counts overlaid on the tissue for representative samples as compared to the protein-coding gene counts.  c , Breakdown of known and novel uTARs identified per cancer sample. The blue region indicates novel uTARs and the other colors indicate an overlap with public datasets (FANTOM, LncBook, NONCODE, GENCODE v.47 novel lncRNA additions and LNCipedia), as well as overlaps in combinations of two, three, four or five of these databases. Bar labels and the gray scale bar on top show the number of uTARs found from each sample. Sample names start with cancer/tissue type abbreviations followed by alphanumeric suffixes. HN, head & neck OPSCC; Kid, kidney; Mel, melanoma; Mel_DN, melanoma dysplastic nevus; MB, medulloblastoma; CP, CRC primary; CM, CRC metastasized.  d , uTAR:gene detection ratio (number of genes versus number of uTARs), per spot across the ST samples. A higher value indicates a higher number of uTARs detected per spot with respect to the number of genes.  e , Characterization of cuTARs based on external evidence of (left) and proportions of cuTARs with several layers of evidence (right).  f , Venn diagram showing the coding-potential-based classification of cuTARs using RNAsamba and CPAT.  g , Prediction of splice sites using AlphaGenome demonstrated for cuTAR213507.   Source data                        The samples used and the number of uTARs identified are summarized in Fig.  1c , with the numbers varying, depending on the cancer type and coverage. For example, a higher number of uTARs were found in breast cancer samples (~45,000–60,000) and one kidney cancer sample (namely KidA) (~45,000), whereas 4,000–25,000 were detected in other samples. Overall, more uTARs were detected with scRNA-seq compared to ST, as scRNA-seq generally captures a higher number of cells. In most samples, approximately 40–60% of the identified uTARs overlapped with lncRNAs cataloged in lncRNA public databases such as FANTOM, LncBook, LNCipedia and NONCODE (Fig.  1c ). Moreover, while our initial analyses used GENCODE v.43 to filter out annotated transcripts, the recent v.47 release has expanded lncRNA annotations  19  . To account for this update, we retained uTARs that overlap lncRNA or noncoding pseudogene annotations in v.47 but were unannotated in v.43. Many of these had been identified by our method, demonstrating transcripts that we identified as unannotated lncRNAs in v.43 are now recognized as lncRNAs in GENCODE v.47. The remaining transcripts are likely novel discoveries not yet reported by other databases and merit further investigation (Fig.  1c ).  The relative uTAR:gene counts for each tissue at Visium spot-level resolution was calculated as the total number of uTARs divided by the total number of genes detected per spot (Fig.  1d ). A higher value indicates a higher number of total uTARs detected per Visium spot with respect to the number of coding genes, as in the melanoma samples (Fig.  1d ); however, this could be due to the lower sample quality (<200 median genes per spot). As the uTARs analyzed in this study span various cancer types and tissues, we merged overlapping uTARs across multiple samples into a single uTAR. These were designated as cancer-associated uTARs (cuTARs) (Supplementary Fig.  4 ) and assigned unique numerical identifiers in our SPanC-Lnc database. The terms uTAR, cuTAR and lncRNA are used interchangeably throughout the paper. A total of 47 cuTARs were expressed on a pan-cancer level (expressed in at least one sample per cancer type in the study) and 1,278 in at least ten cancer types, whereas most of the others exhibited specificity to particular cancer types (Extended Data Fig.  1a,b ). The consistency of detection across different sequencing platforms (ST, 3’ and 5’ scRNA-seq) for melanoma samples was also analyzed. About 1,574 cuTARs were detected in melanoma samples across all the three different platforms (Extended Data Fig.  1c ). Following these findings, we further investigated some of these potential disease-associated candidates in specific cancer types.    Characterization of cuTAR transcripts  To further define cuTAR structure, we overlapped cuTAR coordinates with transcription start site (TSS) annotations from FANTOM, poly-A sites (PAS) and splice sites (Fig.  1e ). They were classified as cuTARs with (1) complete evidence (overlapping with a TSS at the 5′ end and a PAS at the 3′ end within a 1.5-kb window upstream and downstream, respectively); (2) partial evidence comprising of first exons (TSS at the 5′ end and a donor site junction at the 3′ end), internal exons (acceptor site at the 5′ end and a donor site at the 3′ end) and last exons (acceptor site at the 5′ end and PAS at the 3’ end); and (3) incomplete evidence if it overlapped with either TSS or PAS (Fig.  1e ). Overall, 9.07% cuTARs had complete evidence (Fig.  1e ) and 24.9% cuTARs had PAS, last and internal exon evidence, potentially indicating that these transcripts have at least two exons. Overall, 27% cuTARs had only PAS evidence, which is expected as most cuTARs were biased to the 3′ end. To collect further evidence, the cuTARs were overlapped with the new lncRNA annotations from GENCODE v.47 since the release v.43 (Fig.  1e ). Overlapping cuTARs with human permissive enhancers from FANTOM, we found that 3.32% were enhancer-derived lncRNAs (e-lncRNAs) with an enhancer overlap at the 5′ end and 7.29% with an enhancer spanning anywhere along the cuTAR sequence. Additionally, to ensure cuTARs are independent and not potential read-throughs of nearby genes, we labeled those located within 10 kb downstream of coding genes as ‘less confident’ (12.5% of cuTARs).  The sequences were analyzed using CPAT and RNAsamba for coding potential. The CPAT algorithm results are affected by the length of the transcript. RNAsamba is an alternative coding potential calculator that works well on partial-length sequences  20  . RNAsamba identified 97% of all cuTARs to be noncoding. While CPAT filtered out many cuTARs, RNAsamba retained most of them and inferred the coding potential. Overall, 76.6% of cuTARs were predicted to be noncoding using both the tools and 98.3% of the total cuTARs lacked coding potential (Fig.  1f ). The lncRNAs with a coding potential might indicate their role in encoding functional micropeptides, as opposed to necessarily being protein-coding transcripts  21 , 22  . As the cuTARs represent estimated transcript boundaries using data captured from either the 3′ or 5′ ends, the calculated coding potentials may be less accurate than those obtained using the full-length sequence, but they can still provide a meaningful reflection of their coding potential. Moreover, 94.75% of them were at least 200 bp, suggesting that the majority of cuTARs were most likely to be ‘long’ ncRNAs  23  .  Additionally, we predict splice sites utilizing AlphaGenome  24  . To evaluate AlphaGenome predictions, we visualized the  BIRC5  gene (Extended Data Fig.  2a ) and compared the predicted splice sites with the RefSeq exon annotations for the cuTARs that have been annotated in GENCODE v.47 but were unannotated as of v.43 (Extended Data Fig.  2b ). In most cases, predicted splice site peaks were consistent with the annotated exon–intron junctions. With this serving as a performance reference, we were able to predict and suggest potential splice sites in the unannotated and uncharacterized cuTARs (Fig.  1g ).  Conservation and minimum free energy (MFE) are useful metrics for assessing sequence functionality and were calculated for the H&N sample C (HNC). Most top cuTAR candidates had lower conservation than  GAPDH  or the lncRNA  HOTAIR . They also had a stable secondary structure (Supplementary Fig.  5a ).  The genetic-level regulation of the cuTARs through enrichment of eQTL and GWAS SNPs are elaborated in Supplementary Note  1  (Supplementary Figs.  5b  and  6–8 ).    Identification of lncRNAs enriched in cancer tissue regions  Next, we asked whether the cuTAR expression was restricted specifically to the tumor area within the biopsies. Given that lncRNAs can be present in both healthy and tumor tissues, tumor specificity was defined by enrichment within cancerous regions annotated by a pathologist and where histological annotation was unavailable (for example, CP), inferred from tumor-associated gene expression patterns (Fig.  2a ). Top cuTAR candidates for each cancer type were shortlisted based on their detection across various datasets and higher expression in the annotated cancerous regions. The percentage of spots in the cancerous versus normal regions expressing the selected cuTARs in the H&N OPSCC samples were calculated (Fig.  2b ).  Fig. 2   Identification of tumor region specific cuTARs and validation with spatial long-read sequencing and single-cell resolved ST.   a , Tumor regions (dark shaded) in the H&N cancer samples HNB and HNC and CRC primary tumor sample (CP).  b , (From left to right) cuTAR lengths, overlap of cuTARs with that from scRNA-seq data and with lncRNAs from public databases, expression of cuTARs in bulk RNA-seq samples from TCGA (normalized bigWig coverage) and quantification of the cuTARs in the cancerous and normal regions of H&N cancer samples. The cuTARs found across multiple samples are indicated by the sample suffix (_B, _C and _D). The highlighted cuTARs with red boxes indicate the ones with higher expression in the tumor region than the normal region, some of which are shown in  c . These show relatively higher expression in the analyzed H&N cancer samples from TCGA highlighted using the vertical red box.  c , Expression of exemplar cancer region-specific cuTARs projected on the tissues.  d , Validation of cuTARs with ONT and PacBio MAS-seq long-read sequencing for H&N and CRC samples, respectively.  e , uTARs shared across single-cell resolution spatial data from STOmics and Takara Bio Seeker and our Visium/scRNA-seq identified cuTARs. Overall, 83.47% of cuTARs identified using 10x Visium ST and scRNA-seq were also detected with STOmics and Takara Bio Seeker.  f , Expression of cancer-specific cuTARs visualized on STOmics and Takara Bio Seeker samples.   Source data                        The expression of these top cuTAR candidates was detected across many cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)  25   bulk RNA-seq samples. Some cuTARs showed higher expression in the seven TCGA OPSCC samples used, consistent with the observation that all these candidates were tumor-specific in the H&N ST data (Fig.  2b ). Among the cuTARs differentially expressed across these two annotated regions (Supplementary Fig.  9 ), visual examination of gene expression overlaid on the tissues reveal some cuTARs with higher expression in the tumor regions (Fig.  2a,c ). Not only cancer region specificity, but also subclone specificity was observed. The tumor subclones were identified based on inferred copy-number variation using CopyKAT  26   (Extended Data Fig.  3 ).    Confirmation of lncRNA detection using spatial long-read sequencing  Since the 10x Visium protocol captures only the 3′ ends of fragmented transcripts, the actual transcripts are likely longer than the detected cuTAR boundaries. To increase confidence in transcript identification, we applied long-read sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) and PacBio MAS-Seq (Pacific Biosciences) to unfragmented cDNA from 10x Visium libraries. Although these libraries remain 3′ biased, long-read sequencing yields longer fragments, allowing more confident mapping of cuTAR signals than using Visium short read data. We found the signals detected to be consistent across different technologies, suggesting that these cuTARs were likely to be genuine signals rather than artifacts from the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline.  10x Visium unfragmented cDNA libraries from the HNC (OPSCC), SCC and basal cell carcinoma (BCC) samples were used for the ONT experiment. As a representative example, from HNC, we obtained ~16 million ONT reads, with 3,888 spatial barcodes identified by the scNanoGPS pipeline  27  , allowing us to map to 1,028 Visium spots across the tissue. We successfully recovered ~83.6% reads that were complete (with spatial barcode, unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), 3′ adaptors and poly-A/T tails), identifying approximately 985 cuTARs (Supplementary Table  2 ), 960 of which were present in at least three spots overlapping the tissue. This accounts for 31.7% of those detected using 10x Visium, thus validating the detection of uTAR expression from the short-read data. Similar spatial patterns were observed (Fig.  2d ), with up to 38% of spots showing expression in both the technologies and up to 86% for coding genes (Supplementary Note  2  and Supplementary Fig.  10 ). Notably, when we applied the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline directly to the Nanopore BAM files, we identified 32 novel uTARs not detected with the short-read data. In addition, we confirmed signals from the transcriptionally active region (TAR) annotations generated using the 10x Visium data, where 857 ONT uTARs (807 cuTARs) were also detected in the HNC Visium sample. Overall, 92 additional cuTARs detected with ONT were present in our entire database but not in the corresponding Visium sample. To evaluate the results, the consistency of expression patterns for coding genes were also verified (Supplementary Fig.  10 ). There was a substantial overlap of expressing spots across both the platforms for some cuTARs (Extended Data Fig.  4a ). The same analysis was performed for cutaneous SCC and BCC using ONT (Extended Data Fig.  4b,c ).  For the PacBio MAS-Seq long read sequencing run with complementary DNA of CRC samples from the 10x Visium experiment, we generated approximately 1 million HiFi reads. By aligning the reads and tagging them with spatial barcode information, we found up to 1,500 lncRNAs per sample, which accounted for up to ~20% of those detected with 10x Visium (Extended Data Fig.  4d ), thereby also confirming the findings of the 10x Visium Illumina data. We then examined specific cuTARs and found that up to 30% of the spots showed statistically significant consistency in expression for the same set of spots across both the platforms for two CRC-specific cuTARs (Fig.  2d  and Extended Data Fig.  4b,c ) (for example, cuTAR86784, 19%;  P  = 0.011; cuTAR114310, 29%;  P   =  0.014). Overall, we found the PacBio sequencing mapping efficiency was better than that of ONT considering the number of uniquely mapping cuTARs identified for the number of reads captured and processed. More quality control (QC) statistics for long-read spatial sequencing are described in Supplementary Tables  2  and  3 .    Takara Bio Seeker and STOmics spatial data confirmed cuTARs at single-cell resolution  The cuTAR detection at single cell resolution was analyzed with Takara Bio Seeker for one breast cancer and one melanoma sample. We observed consistent expression patterns of coding genes generated using the Takara Bio Seeker pipeline (Extended Data Fig.  5a ) and the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline (Extended Data Fig.  5a ) in the breast cancer sample. Some previously identified breast-cancer-specific cuTARs were also visualized (Extended Data Fig.  5b ). Similarly, annotated genes and melanoma-specific cuTARs were visualized on the melanoma sample (Extended Data Fig.  5c,d ). A spatial and single cell pan-cancer atlas of lncRNAs  The findings of this study have been made publicly available through our database ‘ SPanC-Lnc ’ on AWS cloud (Extended Data Fig.  9 ). A total of 219,442 cuTARs across 13 broad cancer types were identified using scRNA-seq and 10x Visium ST, further validated using five ST platforms. This resource allows users to interactively query lncRNA/cuTAR annotations in a user-friendly UCSC-style genome browser, providing visualizations for cross-cancer expression comparisons, cell-type specificity via UMAP overlays and spatial localization within tumor sections. Users can also retrieve splice junction predictions and associated metadata using the table browser. The metadata includes information about cancer/cell-type specificity, overlap with public lncRNA databases, structural characterization and cross-platform validations. SPanC-Lnc is a large pan-cancer resource of known and new lncRNAs with single cell and spatial contexts. Resources like FANTOM-CAT, LncBook and NONCODE provide lncRNA annotations mostly from bulk RNA-seq data of cell lines and tissues (Supplementary Table  1 ). SPanC-Lnc has lncRNAs with cell type and spatial resolution, lacking from bulk RNA-seq. Recent studies utilizing scRNA-seq and ST data have explored the expression of annotated lncRNAs  5 , 6 , 44 , 45  ; however, information on a pan-cancer scale for potential novel lncRNAs is not available. SPanC-Lnc not only provides annotations and transcript characterization, but also expression comparisons across different cancer types and cell-types and analyzes their potential putative functions. The resource is structured to accommodate incorporation of additional datasets and analytical refinements, and transcript annotations may be further refined as new data become available or as structural and functional validations provide additional evidence. The modular design and documented workflows facilitate transparency, reproducibility and potential future extensions of the atlas.     Discussion  This study utilized advanced transcriptomics technologies for uncovering a diverse repertoire of previously unannotated and/or uncharacterized lncRNAs in cancer. Through integrative analysis across multiple cancer types, we identified lncRNAs exhibiting dynamic expression patterns and tumor-specific spatial distributions, suggesting their potential roles as major regulators in tumorigenesis and cancer progression.  At a structural level, lncRNAs could be derived from enhancers, promoters, pseudogenes or transposons. The lncRNAs derived from the transcription of active enhancers (e-lncRNAs) are known to participate in many cancer-associated biological processes like angiogenesis, proliferation, invasion and metastasis  46 – 49  . At the genetic level, disease-associated GWAS SNPs or eQTLs could regulate nearby protein-coding genes through altering the levels of colocalizing lncRNAs  50  . Spatial autocorrelation with coding genes involved in several cancer-related pathways revealed coexpression of these novel lncRNAs in pathways associated with cell cycle, cellular proliferation, immune response, angiogenesis, hypoxia and metastasis, highlighting their putative involvement in critical biological processes underlying cancer development.  In our study, reads within a 500-bp window were merged and annotated as a single uTAR. While this heuristic simplifies annotation, it introduces potential limitations. For example, a long cuTAR (defined from overlapping uTARs across samples) may represent merged signals from independent transcripts, or adjacent cuTARs may be conflated into a single transcript. This was particularly evident in the higher-resolution STOmics/Takara Bio dataset, where longer transcript boundaries led to the merging of multiple Visium-derived cuTARs into a single STOmics cuTAR. Notably, cuTAR discovery and characterization were based primarily on Visium and scRNA-seq data, where transcript boundaries are shorter and more conservative, reducing the risk of over-merging during novel lncRNA identification. STOmics/Takara Bio data were used for validation rather than discovery, and in many cases the extended boundaries reinforced the presence of a single transcript by extending its annotated range. We prioritized expression specificity, reproducibility and biological association (for example, cancer state, treatment response and cell type) rather than precise transcript boundaries. Consequently, the biological signal and specificity of these cuTARs remain robust despite minor annotation discrepancies. This atlas provides a biologically relevant set of cancer-specific, cell-type-specific and treatment-responsive lncRNAs that already serves as a foundation for biological discovery and can be further refined as transcript annotations improve.  While poly-adenylated lncRNAs were the main focus of this study, other classes of ncRNAs like circular RNAs (circRNAs)  51 , 52  , pre-miRNAs/miRNAs  53  , piRNAs  54 , 55   and non-polyadenylated lncRNAs  56   are also aberrantly expressed in cancers and gene regulation. The identification of these lncRNAs in addition to the new lncRNA panel put forth in this study would serve as a valuable resource for future investigations. Notably, we also added STOmics (random hexamer capture) data to complement polyA-capture methods. We detected 93,255 new uTARs and 105,701 uTARs overlapping with 41,573 entries in databases like LncBook, LNCipedia and NONCODE. Of these, 63,584 uTARs overlap with 32,202 lncRNAs on the same strand. This suggests that some of these uTARs may be non-polyadenylated lncRNAs, making them worthwhile candidates for further investigation in future studies.  A large number of lncRNAs identified from scRNA-seq and ST data can be assigned as highly expressed markers specific to subpopulations of cells, including rare cells. SPanC-Lnc constitutes a scalable resource for investigating fundamental aspects of lncRNA biology, offering new approaches to identifying new lncRNAs and inferring their functions at single-cell and spatial resolution. By systematically comparing lncRNA expression across diverse cellular subpopulations, the discovery framework enables interrogation of cell-type specificity, transcriptional heterogeneity and context-dependent expression patterns that are not accessible through bulk RNA-seq. The integration of spatial information further allows examination of how lncRNA expression varies across tissue architecture, such as tumor cores, immune-rich regions and invasive margins. This spatially resolved view provides an opportunity to study microenvironment-associated transcriptional programs and to generate testable hypotheses about lncRNA regulation in situ, for example through the colocalization and co-regulation of lncRNA with coding genes and pathways. Notably, SPanC-Lnc establishes a standardized computational strategy for integrating single-cell and spatial datasets to annotate, prioritize and visualize lncRNAs across different technology platforms and cancer types. As such, it provides a reference database that can be extended to include additional datasets for more tissues, disease states and emerging single-cell and ST technologies. By enabling systematic exploration of the noncoding transcriptome at a cellular resolution, this resource facilitates mechanistic studies aimed at defining the regulatory principles governing lncRNA expression and functions.    Methods   Primary datasets   Spatial transcriptomics datasets across different cancers  Previously published in-house datasets from fresh frozen tissues of different cancer types (kidney  57  , SCC, BCC  58  , H&N OPSCC  30  , medulloblastoma  42  , CRC  59   and breast cancers  60  ) and clinical formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) biopsies of melanoma  61   were used in this study (10x Visium poly-A capture). One healthy tissue from kidney was also used (KidB_N). Previously published in-house melanoma datasets  61   and other publicly available datasets of ovarian and prostate cancers from the 10x Visium FFPE probe hybridization based capture were used as the control in our initial phase (published elsewhere)  62  . As this approach relies on predefined gene-targeting probes, novel ncRNAs are generally not captured, although off-target lncRNA detection has been reported  62  . The coverage of the samples used in this study was an average of 100 million reads captured from about 2,000 spots, whereas for the in-house kidney and breast cancer datasets it was 100–300 million reads. Shown in detail are the results for a few cancer types (including H&N cancer, breast cancer and medulloblastoma) of the in-house spatial and public melanoma scRNA-seq datasets.     Single-cell sequencing data  Datasets from 10x Genomics, including glioblastoma, breast cancer (3’ scRNA-seq), ovarian, pancreatic, kidney cancer, melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (5’ scRNA-seq) were used  63 – 69  .  Other previously published datasets were also used to analyze lncRNA expressions at a cell-type-specific level. These included 3′-sequencing datasets of acral and cutaneous melanoma from the study  PRJNA862451  (ref.   70  ), peripheral blood mononuclear cells from Merkel cell carcinoma (SRR7722937)  71  , patients with H&N cancer (SRR13418965, SRR13419137 and SRR13419168)  72   and 5′-sequencing datasets of tissue biopsies from patients with BCC. This included data before and after anti-PD-1 therapy from three patients (SRX5128480, SRX5128482, SRX5128486, SRX5128489, SRX5128506 and SRX5128507) out of 12 patients in the original study ( GSE123814 )  73  .    Detection of potential novel lncRNAs using an HMM-based approach  The method described by Wang et al.  10   as the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline was adopted to identify TARs. The pipeline uses an R package GroHMM  74   that utilizes a two-state hidden Markov model (HMM) to classify regions in an aligned genome as transcriptionally active or not, based on the read coverage in each bin. The position sorted BAM files generated by the 10x SpaceRanger pipeline (SpaceRanger 1.3.0 and 2.0.1 using default parameters) were used as inputs to the pipeline (outputs from 10x Cell Ranger were used for scRNA-seq data). By default, it splits the genome into nonoverlapping bins of 50 bp and is called transcriptionally active if at least three reads were detected in that bin and were labeled as TARs. TARs found within 500 bp apart were merged into one unit. One of the limitations of this approach is that we might wrongly identify two different but adjacent transcripts as a single transcript. The regions identified were then overlapped with reference gene annotations in a strand-specific manner (reference annotations from GENCODE v.43 were used). The TARs overlapping with existing gene annotations (even a few base pairs of overlap is considered ‘annotated’ to account for extended gene boundaries) were labeled aTARs (annotated TARs) and the ones falling outside gene boundaries were called uTARs (unannotated TARs). We rule out the unannotated transcripts found on the opposite strand to that of an annotated transcript for this initial phase of the study. A count matrix of the TARs is generated with Drop-Seq tools DigitalExpression function  75  .    Analysis of sequences for coding potential, conservation and stability  To make sure that the identified transcripts were noncoding, the coding potential was analyzed using CPAT  76   and RNAsamba  20  . The FASTA sequences of the cuTARs were extracted using BEDtools  77   getfasta. CPAT was then run using the inbuilt model for the human genome. A human coding probability (HCP) cutoff of 0.364 was used as described in the tool’s documentation. HCP ≥ 0.364 indicates a coding sequence, whereas HCP < 0.364 indicates a noncoding sequence  76  . On the other hand, RNAsamba uses a neural network architecture to classify transcripts as coding or noncoding solely based on sequence information, and is robust to limitations such as truncated open reading frames, and hence more reliable.  Various metrics can help infer the functional significance of a sequence. One such metric is the conservation score, where highly evolutionarily conserved sequences tend to be associated with common essential functions across organisms, while less conserved sequences may exhibit specific functions in an organism. The conservation of the sequences were calculated using the phastCons BigWig files comprising the phastCons scores for multiple alignments of 29 primate/mammalian genome sequences to the human genome GRCh38/hg38 build ( http://hgdownload.cse.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg38/phastCons30way/hg38.phastCons30way.bw )  78  . The BEDtools bigWigAverageOverBed function was used extract the conservation score for each specified coordinate in a bed file.  MFE is another measure for potential functionality. In general, the lower the MFE, the more stable the secondary structure of the transcript is and hence more likely to be functional. MFE was calculated for each cuTAR in the HNC sample with RNAfold (v.2.6.4)  79   using default parameters. The most stable secondary structure is predicted.    Characterization of structure and potential functional implications  The identified uTARs were overlapped with TSS and enhancer data from FANTOM for window sizes ranging within 1.5 kb at the 5′ end. PAS data from the PolyASite database ( https://polyasite.unibas.ch/ ) curated from 3′-end scRNA-seq data was used to support the 3′ end of our cuTARs. Splice junction data from Intropolis  80   ( http://intropolis.rail.bio ), which is a database of splice junctions from analyzing 21,504 human samples sequenced on Illumina was also used to identify splice sites and hence characterize the structure of the identified cuTARs. To further validate our lncRNA identification, the cuTARs were overlapped with the new lncRNA annotations from GENCODE v.47 since release v.43, confirming that these are lncRNAs that were identified by the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline before GENCODE annotated them as lncRNAs. Additionally, we also predict splice sites utilizing AlphaGenome  24  , a deep-learning-based tool used to predict several functional genomic features and events. It has been shown that AlphaGenome predicts splicing events with a high accuracy (Pearson correlation of up to 0.82).  The identified cuTAR reads were also overlapped with trait-associated SNPs from the GWAS catalog (all associations v.1.0.2)  81   and with GTEx CAVIAR eQTLs from the UCSC  82   table browser (downloaded on 23 August 2025)  83   with a window size of 100 kb using BEDtools to propose potential genetic-level regulation based on colocalizing features. Three sets of an equal number of random coding regions were considered and the overlap of eQTLs were calculated. There was a markedly higher overlap of cuTARs than with three sets of randomly chosen coding regions. The eQTLs overlapped with both the pan-cancer cuTARs and the cancer-specific cuTARs were identified using direct overlap (BEDtools intersect) and window sizes of 10 kb and 100 kb. The genes associated with these colocalized eQTLs were then queried in enrichR for enriched pathways, GO terms, cell-types and tissues, the significance of which were computed using Fisher’s exact test  84  .  The identified cuTARs were overlapped with active enhancers from FANTOM  85   to identify e-lncRNAs using BEDtools (500-bp window size at the 5′ end and also for the entire length of the cuTAR). These can also provide important clues about the regulatory mechanisms and potential functions of these transcripts, helping to shed light on the complex regulatory networks that govern gene expression.    Identification of cancer-specific lncRNAs  Tumor regions were identified using pathologist-provided annotations where available (for example, HNB, HNC), or inferred based on gene expression profiles when such annotations were not available (for example, CP). For analyses requiring cell-type classification (for example, BreastA), scType  86   was employed. Pathologist annotations were exported via Loupe Browser (10x Genomics) and incorporated into downstream analyses. The cuTARs differentially expressed across the annotated cancer and normal regions were identified using Seurat v.4.3 and processed using SCTransform. For FindAllMarkers function, the parameters min.pct was set to 0.1 and logfc.threshold varied between 0.1–0.25 depending on the sample analyzed. The percentage of spots in the cancerous versus healthy regions expressing the selected cuTARs were also calculated.  Few cuTARs from H&N cancer samples were shortlisted as the cuTARs of interest that could be the top potential functional candidates. They were chosen as they were (1) detected in all H&N OPSCC samples; (2) longer than 1,000 bp; (3) absent from standard annotations (GENCODE v.43) but supported by entries in other lncRNA-specific databases; and (4) differentially expressed in the cancerous region of the tissue. To be more confident about the chosen regions, we also checked their coverages in bulk RNA-seq datasets from TCGA and the scRNA-seq dataset of HNC and checked if they were detected. The bigwig RNA-seq coverage files for 96 random TCGA samples were downloaded using recount. The cuTAR coverages were extracted from these files using bigWigAverageOverBed function from UCSC Tools for the specified boundaries in a .bed file. TMM normalization was performed on the raw coverage (counts) using edgeR. By analyzing coverage, gene expression levels can be inferred. Regions with higher coverage indicate higher expression levels of the corresponding cuTARs.    Confirmation of detected signals using long-read sequencing and spatial technologies with single-cell resolution   Oxford Nanopore  Long-read sequencing with ONT was performed using the 10x Visium biotinylated 3′ cDNA libraries to validate the detection and expression patterns of the identified potential lncRNAs using PromethION flow cells. SQK-LSK110 and EXP-NBD kits from ONT were used to generate the libraries for the H&N sample C (HNC). Sequence runs were generated using super-accurate basecalling setting with MinKNOW v.22.12.5 and Guppy v.6.4.6 (flow cell type FLO-PRO002). The nanopore run generated ~16 million reads. To demultiplex the reads based on the spatial barcode, scNanoGPS  27   was used. Some changes were made to the default parameters of the pipeline with respect to the scan region, which was set to 1,000 bp as the 3′ adaptors were found that many bases away owing to longer chimeras. The lncRNAs were then identified using a modified version of the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline, as scNanoGPS generates individual alignment files for each spatial barcode identified, rather than an individual BAM file with reads tagged with spatial/cell and UMI barcodes. Featurecounts  87   was used to generate the uTAR expression matrix. GTF annotations of the TARs from the corresponding 10x Visium dataset was also used to generate the count matrix. The identified spatial barcodes were matched with those from the 10x Visium barcode list from the tissue_positions_list.csv in the SpaceRanger output of the corresponding Visium data and only those with tissues placed on them were retained. The coordinates of the matched barcodes were also extracted from the aforementioned csv file. The expression of some potential candidates were visualized using stlearn  88   and was compared to that of the previously generated short-read data.  Further, the experiment was also performed for skin cancer samples. SQK-NBD-114.24 kit, native barcoding kit 24 V14, was used to prepare libraries for the SCC and BCC samples, which were sequenced on PromethION P24 device using R10 flow cell (FLO-PRO114M). Sequence bases were called during the sequencing run in fast-base-calling mode using PromethION software release 23.11.4 (minknow-core-promethion 5.8.3, Dorado v.7.2.13). Then, re-basecalling was performed in super-accuracy mode using Dorado (v.0.5.1). Median read length, read length N50 and median PHRED scores were computed from re-basecalled FASTQ files (Q > 10) using NanoStat (v.1.6.0)  89  . The re-basecalled reads were subsequently processed using the same downstream workflow described for HNC, including scNanoGPS analysis and cuTAR identification and visualization.     PacBio  Full-length Visium cDNA libraries were used for HiFi sequencing. Multiplexed array sequencing (MAS-Seq), a library preparation method that concatenates cDNA molecules for long-read sequencing, was used following the 10x Single Cell 3′ kit protocol (PN: 102-678-600-REV03). After cDNA amplification, cleanup and QC of 10x Visium, 225 pM cDNA per library with concentration of 23 ng μl −1  were pooled for sequencing. First, the template switching ligoonucleotide priming artifacts during cDNA synthesis were removed using biotinylated primers. Next, DNA fragments containing orientation-specific MAS segmentation adaptor sequences were generated by performing 16 parallel cDNA amplification reactions. MAS enzyme was used to create single-stranded extensions to enable directional assembly of cDNA segments into a linear array. After DNA damage repair and nuclease treatment, cDNA cleanup was performed with 1.2× SMRTbell beads.  Further, the pbcromwell workflow of SMRTlink Tools (v.12.0.0)  90   was used for to process the HiFi BAM files. With the aligned genome file from Minimap2, the TAR-scRNA-seq pipeline was run and the cuTAR expression was overlaid on the tissues and compared to that of Visium.    STOmics  Sample preparation and library construction were performed following the manufacturer’s protocol (STOmics Stereo-seq FFPE kit). In brief, stereo-seq chip slides were equilibrated to room temperature and rinsed with nuclease-free water. FFPE tissue blocks were sectioned at 5-µm thickness and mounted onto stereo-seq chip N slides (STOmics Stereo-seq OMNI). Mounted slides were baked at 42 °C for 3 h, followed by overnight incubation at 37 °C. Mounted slides were subjected to deparaffinization, H&E staining and imaging, followed by de-crosslinking to reverse formalin-induced crosslinks. Tissue sections were permeabilized to release RNA molecules, which were hybridized in situ to spatially barcoded free probes embedded on the stereo-seq chip surface, enabling unbiased capture of total RNA. On-chip reverse transcription, ligation and cDNA release were performed, after which cDNA was amplified, purified and converted into sequencing-ready libraries. Libraries were sequenced on the DNBSEQ-T7 platform (MGI Tech) and raw reads were processed using the Stereo-seq Analysis Workflow (SAW; v.8.1.3) for QC, alignment and generation of spatially resolved gene expression matrices integrated with H&E-stained images, enabling downstream analyses such as spatial clustering, cell-type annotation and visualization of coding and noncoding RNA expression at single-cell and subcellular resolution.    Takara Bio Seeker  The Takara Bio Seeker raw and processed data for human breast cancer and melanoma samples were acquired from Curio Bioscience, now part of Takara Bio USA.    RT–qPCR  Six cDNA samples from the 10x Visium libraries, including H&N samples (HNB and HNC), SCC, BCC and CRC (CP and CM) were tested for seven potential lncRNAs (cuTAR100897, cuTAR121087, cuTAR170206, cuTAR17878, cuTAR213507, cuTAR234975 and cuTAR70920).  GAPDH , a housekeeping gene and  KRT18 , an epithelial marker were used as positive controls. Two negative controls NEG1 and NEG2 were designed to target genomic regions around the centromere that do not code for RNA, hence controls for any genomic DNA contamination. H 2 O was used as a nontemplate negative control. Overall, 12 primers were designed to target seven cuTARs (Supplementary Table  4 ). The primers were designed in such a way that they did not have any off-targets using the sequence information of the HNC sample. qPCR Master Mix was prepared for each sample following the KAPA SYBR FAST qPCR kit guide to allow each well to contain 1 μl of 10 ng μl −1  cDNA, 5 μl KAPA SYBR FAST qPCR Master Mix (2×) (Roche), 0.2 μl ROX Low Reference Dye (50×) (Roche) and 3.4 μl of RNase-free water. As  GAPDH  was an endogenous control, the template for this primer was further diluted 1:8 to ensure that it was within a comparable quantifiable range. Then, 9.6 μl of the qPCR Master Mix was loaded into each well on the 96-well quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) plate before 0.4 μl of 10 nM respective lncRNA primer pairs were added. The qPCR reaction was performed with the following protocol using the ViiA7 96-well Real-Time PCR System with High Resolution Melt (Applied Biosystems); initial denaturation (98 °C for 3 min), two-step amplification (98 °C for 5 s and 63 °C for 30 s) for a total of 35 cycles with the melting curve method. The expression was calculated using the formula  C  KRT18  × CT KRT18  =  C  cuTAR  × CT cuTAR , where CT KRT18  and CT cuTAR  represent the cycle threshold (CT) values for the positive control gene KRT18 and the cuTAR target, respectively, and  C  KRT18  and  C  cuTAR  denote their corresponding normalized expression levels, calculated as described below.  The CT was normalized with that of one of the positive controls  KRT18  such that  C  KRT18  = 1. The cuTAR expression was calculated as  C  cuTAR  = 1 × CT KRT18 /CT cuTAR . The average was used for two primers targeting a same cuTAR. The expression was visualized on a heatmap (Supplementary Fig.  12 ).    Spatial autocorrelation of lncRNAs with genes relevant to cancer  SpatialDE  91   was used to identify spatially variable features. The significant spatially variable cuTARs and the top chosen candidates chosen for the H&N cancer samples were further used to measure pairwise spatial autocorrelation with coding genes using bivariate Moran’s  I  using Python scripts. Several hallmark genes relevant to cancer were retrieved from gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-MsigDB  92   and were used for the analysis. The spots showing (1) high expression of both the gene and the cuTAR were categorized as HH; (2) spots with gene expression and no cuTAR expression as LH; (3) ones with cuTAR expression and lack of gene expression as HL; (4) no expression of both features as LL; and (5) NS for spots with insignificant Moran’s  I . The cuTARs showing high spatial correlation (more than 50 HH spots) with genes of different hallmarks were calculated to identify the more functionally relevant cuTARs and the pathways involved. Moran’s  I  was calculated in a simple format using the formula below:       \documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

It measures bivariate spatial correlation for expression values of an lncRNA (cuTAR) ( t ) and a gene ( t  − 1) across all spots with the standardized expression of the cuTAR in the central spots/cells  i , and the standardized expression of the gene in the neighboring spots/cells  j . Spatial weights (w  ij  ) represent the proximity between spatial spots/cells  i  and  j . These weights are defined based on spatial contiguity where  w   i    j   > 0 if  j  is a neighbor of  i  defined by sharing a border or nearest in proximity, and 0 if otherwise; the total sum of the neighbor weights for each central spot is 1. With this,  I  T  is 1 if all neighboring spots/cells  z   j , t  − 1  have the same standardized expression value of the gene with the standardized expression value of the cuTAR at the central spot  z   i , t  . Therefore,  I  T  = 1 indicates that the value of a gene has a high spatial autocorrelation with the cuTAR based on the expression of values of neighboring spots, suggesting that the gene and cuTAR are spatially dependent and tend to colocalize across the tissue.  The coexpression network analysis was performed using hdWGCNA  93   for merged gene-cuTAR count matrices processed using Seurat v.4.1. The spatial regions of interest were the tumor regions marked by a pathologist for the sample HNC and based on Moran’s  I  for BreastA.    Interaction with RBPs and colocalization  Machine-learning models that have been trained using known lncRNA–protein interactions can be used to predict interaction of novel lncRNAs with proteins, adding another layer of information for potential functionality. HLPI-Ensemble, which adopts the ensemble strategy based on three mainstream machine-learning algorithms of support vector machines, random forests and extreme gradient boosting was used to predict the interaction of top cuTARs with RBPs. Further, the spatial colocalization of cuTARs with their interacting RBP-encoding genes and with genes reported to be associated with those RBPs was visualized.    Identification of cell-type-specific lncRNAs and their response to therapy  The melanoma scRNA-seq dataset from the study  PRJNA862451  (ref.   70  ) was used to identify cell-type-specific lncRNAs and their response to therapy. The dataset included acral and cutaneous melanoma samples. The coding gene count matrices of four acral and one cutaneous melanoma samples (10x Chromium V2 chemistry) were integrated using the Seurat workflow and clustering was performed. Cell-type clusters were annotated using canonical markers described in the original study: melanocytes ( MITF ,  PMEL ,  TYR ,  DCT ,  MLANA ,  PMEL ,  APOC1  and  S100A1 ), cycling melanoma cells ( UBE2C ,  NUSAP1 ,  MKI67  and  CENPF ), endothelial cells ( VWF  and  PECAM1 ), fibroblasts ( COL3A1 ,  COL1A2 ,  COL1A1  and  LUM ), CD8 +  T cells ( CD8A ,  HAVCR2 ,  LAG3 ,  PD1 ,  TIGIT ,  CTLA4  and  HOPX ), CD4 +  T cells ( CD4 ,  FOXP3  and  IL2 ), monocytes ( CD14 ,  LYZ ,  CD74 ,  CD68  and  CD79A ), B cells ( MS4A1 ), natural killer (NK) cells ( GNLY ,  FGFBP2 ,  FCGR3A ,  KLRD1  and  KLRF1 ), NK-like T cells ( CD3E ,  CD3D ,  GZMB ,  XCL2 ,  IFNG ,  CCL4 ,  NKG7 ,  GZMA  and  GZMK ) and macrophages ( CD68 ,  CD163 ,  CD14 ,  CD11b ,  CD206 ,  CD80 ,  CD86 ,  CD16 ,  CD64 ,  CCL18 ,  CD115 ,  CD11c ,  CD32 ,  HLA-DR ,  MRC1 ,  MSR1 ,  GCA  and  Pf4 ).  The cell barcode and its corresponding cell-type identity were used as metadata for the differential expression analysis of the potential lncRNAs. Differential expression analysis was performed by the pseudobulk approach using edgeR. The model was built as design <-model.matrix(~celltype + sample) to identify cell-type-specific lncRNAs accounting for sample batch effects. For the Manhattan plot, the FoldChange function of Seurat was used to find the upregulated genes and cuTARs in melanoma and cycling melanoma cells compared to the other immune cells.  Further there was only one acral melanoma sample for which data were collected before and after anti-PD-1 treatment. The differentially expressed genes and lncRNAs in the tumor cells with respect to the other cells were identified. Ten pseudoreplicates of 50 cells per cell type were created and their aggregated expression across cell types was visualized. As a positive control, marker genes for melanoma were also visualized. Multiple hypothesis testing was controlled using Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction for any DE analysis.    Response to drug in medulloblastoma PDOX models  In-house Visium medulloblastoma data as described by Vo et al.  42   were also analyzed. In brief, medulloblastoma (SHH MB) tissue from a 4.9-year-old patient was used to generate a PDOX line by implanting tumor cells in the cerebellum of immunocompromised NSG mice within hours of surgical removal from the patient and propagating them from mouse to mouse exclusively without in vitro passaging, as previously described. Two tumor-bearing mice were treated with palbociclib hydrochloride (Pfizer) and the rest were untreated. The raw Visium data were processed using a human–mouse hybrid reference as the tissue comprised the human tumor and the mouse brain tissues. These treated and untreated samples were analyzed for lncRNAs in this study and those significantly differentially expressed between the tumor regions of the treated and untreated groups were identified. DE analysis was performed with each sample as pseudobulks using edgeR and two treated samples were compared to two untreated tumor samples. In addition to the top statistically significant ( P adj < 0.05) differentially expressed cuTARs, several medulloblastoma-specific cuTARs (cuTAR290541, cuTAR78711 and cuTAR276859) are also shown, as they exhibited reproducible upregulation in untreated tumors and cancer-specific expression patterns, and had significant FDR-corrected  P  values when analyzed with increased sampling resolution in the pseudobulk analysis.    Xenium in situ experimental validation of cuTARs  A total of 76 cuTARs were chosen for validation on the Xenium in situ platform to verify their cancer-type specificity as observed using 10x Visium. Five genomic DNA regions around centromeres that do not transcribe into RNA were chosen as a negative control set to prove that the detected cuTAR signals were not noise from genomic DNA but true RNA transcripts. The sequences for probe designing were selected based on performing multiple sequence alignment using ClustalW  94   across the in-house Visium, spatial long read and scRNA samples, and extracting the most represented sequences. The sequences in FASTA format were sent to the 10x Bioinformatics team, who applied their advanced pipeline to design probes for target domains, screening for off-targets (Supplementary Table  5 ).  FFPE tissue blocks of two H&N OPSCC, three melanoma, two breast cancer, four CRC and two glioblastoma samples were sectioned at a thickness of 5 μm and mounted onto Xenium slides, in accordance with the FFPE tissue preparation guide (10x Genomics,  CG000578 , Rev B). In situ hybridization was carried out overnight using 380 probes from the pre-designed Xenium Immuno Oncology Panel (10x Genomics) and from the add-on custom panel of 76 cuTARs and 19 coding genes not represented in the base panel. 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining was used to label nuclei, which were used for the estimation of cell boundaries (10x Genomics,  CG000582 , Rev D). Following completion of the run, H&E staining was conducted on the same tissue region. The Xenium samples from each cancer type were preprocessed individually using Seurat version 5.0. During the QC step, cells with zero expression across all genes were filtered out. Normalization was performed using the SCTransform function. Sample batch correction was performed using RunHarmony(), followed by principal-component analysis using the top 30 principal components. Further, the cancer cells and other cells in the microenvironment were annotated by using the label transfer approach using published and well-annotated single-cell datasets of the respective cancer types for H&N  95  , CRC  96  , breast cancer  97  , GBM  98   and an in-house annotated scRNA-seq dataset for melanoma  58  . To focus on cancer-specific signal and account for variation across diverse tissue architectures, downstream analyses were restricted to predicted tumor-like cells, enriching for the malignant compartment within the spatial tissues. Cancer-type specificity of candidate cuTARs was assessed using edgeR, with tumor-like cells pseudo-bulked per patient to generate sample-level profiles. Tissue-specific expression patterns were visualized via heatmaps to confirm that cuTARs recapitulate cancer-type specificity in Xenium data, consistent with patterns identified from Visium and single-cell RNA-seq analyses.    Survival analysis with TCGA data  Survival analysis was performed by dividing the samples from TCGA into low- and high-cuTAR-expressing groups to see whether any cuTAR could predict survival and thus be used as a prognostic marker. From the TCGA metadata, ‘days_to_last_follow_up’ (for alive patients) and ‘days_to_death’ (for the deceased) were used to define overall survival. Survival analysis was performed using overall survival time and event status, with cuTAR expression strata as the sole covariate. The statistics were implemented using the survdiff() function from the survival R package (v.3.7-0)  99  . For  BIRC5  in Fig.  6d , the plot and the data were obtained from cBioPortal  100   (on 13 December 2025).    Interactive website for annotations and visualization  The findings of this study have been made available for users to browse through the annotations and to visualize coding gene and cuTAR expression on tissue images. The Angular 13.3 web site is hosted using AWS Amplify. It uses a GitHub repository for version control, AWS Code Build to generate the production artifacts (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) and uses AWS Cloudfront CDN ( https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/features/ ) to distribute these globally. Libraries used include TypeScript v.4.6 and Node v.10.8.1. The backend web service is running the Django v.5.0 web framework on Python v.3.10, using the slim version of Debian Bookworm ( https://hub.docker.com/_/debian ). This is deployed on AWS Lambda instances provisioned with 4.5 GB of RAM connected to an AWS elastic file system for accessing HDF5 and SQLite 3 files used during querying. The Python libraries used include AnnData 0.10, h5py 3.11.0, numba 0.59.1, numpy 1.26.4, pandas 2.2.2, scanpy 1.10.1, scipy 1.13.1 and seaborn 0.13.2. For visualization of expressions, Python scripts were used in the backend with preloaded AnnData objects for each sample (.h5ad files). The website will be updated whenever new samples or annotations are generated.    Ethics approval  All samples were approved for research under ethical approval numbers 2018000165 and 2017000318 by the University of Queensland’s Human Research Ethics Committees. evidence_text:
High-definition spatial transcriptomic profiling of immune cell populations in colorectal cancer. A comprehensive understanding of cellular behavior and response to the tumor microenvironment (TME) in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains elusive. Here, we introduce the high-definition Visium spatial transcriptomic technology (Visium HD) and investigate formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded human CRC samples (n = 5). We demonstrate the high sensitivity, single-cell-scale resolution and spatial accuracy of Visium HD, generating a highly refined whole-transcriptome spatial profile of CRC samples. We identify transcriptomically distinct macrophage subpopulations in different spatial niches with potential pro-tumor and anti-tumor functions via interactions with tumor and T cells. In situ gene expression analysis validates our findings and localizes a clonally expanded T cell population close to macrophages with anti-tumor features. Our study demonstrates the power of high-resolution spatial technologies to understand cellular interactions in the TME and paves the way for larger studies that will unravel mechanisms and biomarkers of CRC biology, improving diagnosis and disease management strategies. Main  CRC accounted for 9.4% of cancer-related deaths (0.9 million) in 2020, and its global incidence is predicted to double by 2035 (refs.   1 , 2  ). Its poor 5-year survival rate highlights the need for better early detection and prognostic biomarkers for future disease management  3  . Growing evidence suggests that tumor heterogeneity is best described at the transcriptome level, rather than with classical histopathological or mutation-centered disease classifications  4  . Technologies that refine our understanding of the TME, including the diverse roles of innate and adaptive immune responses and cellular crosstalk in CRC, have the potential to inform better clinical intervention strategies.  Sequencing-based genomic technologies have played an important role in building our knowledge of CRC biology  4 – 7  . However, bulk sequencing, which involves averages data from cells and tissues, is confounded by the complexities of the TME and intratumor heterogeneity. Single-cell transcriptomic (single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq)) technologies have partially filled this gap and allowed for detailed exploration of the cell types within the TME in CRC  8 – 16  . Although these studies add critical single-cell-level resolution to our understanding of CRC, they lack any information about the cellular organization within the tissue. Spatial transcriptomics offers a solution. Several commercial technologies are currently available, including Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium v2’, 10x Genomics), STOmics (BGI) and Curio Seeker (Curio Bioscience). Other published methods include Seq-Scope  17  , Nova-ST  18  , Open-ST  19  , HDST  20  , DBiT-seq  21  , Pixel-seq  22   and XYZeq  23  . These methods have enabled the localization of cell types within tissues, which is critical for understanding the interaction between cells in the TME of CRC  24 – 27  . However, these technologies lack resolution at the single-cell scale or are typically only compatible with freshly frozen tissues, and, as such, a deep understanding of tumor organization based on readily available biobanked samples remains elusive.  Here, we introduce Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium HD’), a whole-transcriptome assay with single-cell-scale resolution compatible with freshly frozen, fixed frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples. The Visium HD slides provide a dramatically increased oligonucleotide barcode density (~11,000,000 continuous 2-µm features in a 6.5 × 6.5-mm Visium HD capture area, compared to ~5,000 55-µm features with gaps between the equivalent Visium v2 capture area), generating data that can be binned in square features. We demonstrate the use of Visium HD as a discovery platform by profiling CRC FFPE tissue blocks from multiple patients. The single-cell-scale resolution of Visium HD allowed us to map distinct populations of immune cells, specifically macrophages and T cells, and evaluate DGE at the tumor boundary. We also generated a multi-patient single-cell reference dataset from a larger cohort of FFPE samples and used it to annotate deconvolved Visium HD data bins, validating the cell type populations identified by Visium HD and subsequently using the integrated data to comprehensively map the cellular composition and molecular signatures of the TME in CRC. Leveraging the high resolution of Visium HD, we examined the cells at the immediate periphery (within 50 µm) of the tumor. This allowed us to spatially map distinct macrophage subpopulations to specific tumor regions, to compare their transcriptomic profiles, which indicate that they may exert pro-tumor roles via different pathways, and to characterize cell–cell interactions. To validate the spatial accuracy of Visium HD, we analyzed a subset of genes using an independent spatial technology (Xenium In Situ Gene Expression  28  ). We confirmed the presence of the two pro-tumor macrophage subpopulations in different tumor niches and pinpointed the location of the T cells within the TME. We also detected a clonally expanded T cell population and the microenvironment in which it resides, revealing a macrophage-containing niche with anti-tumor features.  Our study underscores the importance of using high-resolution spatial technologies in exploring the heterogeneity of cancer biology. These advanced tools are crucial for precisely mapping diverse immune cell niches and elucidating the complex interactions between these cells and their microenvironment. Spatial technologies provide a detailed understanding of spatial variations in cell types, their subpopulations and cell-to-cell relationships, which are key to developing targeted therapies and personalized treatment approaches. The combination of whole-transcriptome and targeted in situ spatial technologies used in our investigation provides a deep insight into the complex and dynamic nature of the TME, highlighting the importance of spatial context in understanding cancer heterogeneity and disease progression.    Results  Visium HD enables transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression analysis at single-cell scale. Gene expression is measured by the capture of ligated probe pairs targeting the whole protein-coding transcriptome. We profiled tumor biopsies from five patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma, in addition to normal adjacent tissue (NAT) from three of these patients (Table  1 ). Serial sections of FFPE tissues were used to benchmark the technology performance or to explore the TME using Visium HD. Additionally, selected serial sections were used to generate an scRNA-seq dataset and for in situ gene expression analysis (Fig.  1 ). Fig. 1   Analysis of CRC and NAT samples using Visium HD.  Serial tissue sections were taken from colorectal adenocarcinoma (CRC,  n  = 5 samples) and NAT ( n  = 3 samples) FFPE blocks. A subset of samples were selected and analyzed with the Visium HD assay ( n  = 3 CRC and  n  = 2 NAT samples). Sections from the same FFPE blocks were assayed with scRNA-seq (Chromium Single Cell Gene Expression Flex;  n  = 8). Serial sections were analyzed with Xenium In Situ Gene Expression ( n  = 4 CRC samples) and assayed via the Visium v2 assay ( n  = 1 CRC and  n  = 2 NAT samples). Single-cell data were used to create a reference dataset for cell type annotation. In situ data were used for validation of the findings from the Visium HD data and for subsequent analyses. Technology performance comparisons were made using data from matched datasets.                    Visium HD specifications and performance  The Visium HD capture array consists of 2 × 2-µm squares of uniquely barcoded oligonucleotides directly adjacent to each other on the slide, resulting in a continuous lawn of capture oligonucleotides. This represents an increase of several orders of magnitude in barcode complexity over earlier Visium slides, which have 55-µm circular capture areas with a 100-µm center to center gaps between them (Fig.  2a,b ). For downstream analysis, the Space Ranger (version 3.0) pipeline outputs the raw 2-µm data and data binned at 8- and 16-µm resolution. Unless otherwise described, we used the 8-µm binned data in our analyses.
